## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 50 million daily active users, of whom 20% open a document with at least one other concurrent editor
- An actively-typing user generates roughly 5 edit operations (keystrokes/edits) per second in bursts while typing
- Average concurrent editors per actively co-edited document is 3
- Each edit operation, once encoded (position, character, author, version vector or similar), is about 100 bytes

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Concurrently co-edited documents at peak:** 50,000,000 * 20% = 10 million users in shared sessions; 10,000,000 / 3 average editors per doc ≈ 3.3 million concurrently co-edited documents at peak
- **Edit operations generated per second, cluster-wide:** 10,000,000 concurrent editors, but only a fraction typing at any instant, say 10% actively typing at once = 1,000,000 users * 5 ops/sec = 5 million edit ops/sec at peak across the whole system, this is a high-fan-in write rate
- **Broadcast fan-out per edit:** Each edit op is broadcast to the other ~2 co-editors on that document (3 editors - 1 author), so 5,000,000 ops/sec * 2 ≈ 10 million broadcast messages/sec, each tiny (~100 bytes), meaning message rate, not bandwidth, is the real load
- **Bandwidth for edit broadcast:** 10,000,000 messages/sec * 100 bytes ≈ 1 GB/sec cluster-wide, trivial compared to the message-rate/connection-count challenge of maintaining millions of live WebSocket connections

*Capacity Takeaway:* The driving constraint here is not bandwidth (edit operations are tiny) but the sheer number of persistent, low-latency connections and small, frequent messages: millions of concurrently open WebSocket connections each needing sub-second delivery is a connection-management and fan-out problem first, and a data-volume problem a distant second.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Each client applies its own edits locally and instantly (so typing never
waits on the network), while simultaneously sending each edit operation to
a document-editing server over a persistent WebSocket connection. The
server assigns the operation a place in that document's ordered operation
log, transforms or merges it against any operations it hasn't yet seen from
other clients (this is the OT/CRDT layer), and broadcasts the resolved
operation to every other connected client on that document. Every client,
including the one that authored the change, applies operations from the
server in the same resolved form, which is what guarantees convergence:
everyone ends up replaying the same sequence of transformed operations
regardless of the order their local edits actually happened in. Periodic
snapshots let the server (and reconnecting clients) avoid replaying the
full history from scratch.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Real-time edit propagation across editors

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    clientA["Client A"]:::client
    clientB["Client B"]:::client
    serverA["Edit Server 1"]:::server
    serverB["Edit Server 2"]:::server
    pubsub>"Pub/Sub Bus"]:::queue
    oplog[("Operation Log DB")]:::db
    snapshot["Snapshot Store"]:::server
    clientA -->|"op via WebSocket"| serverA
    clientB -->|"op via WebSocket"| serverB
    serverA -.->|"publish op"| pubsub
    pubsub -.->|"deliver op"| serverB
    serverB -->|"push transformed op"| clientB
    serverA -->|"append op"| oplog
    oplog -.->|"periodic compaction"| snapshot
```

#### Operational Transformation vs CRDT

| Operational Transformation | CRDT |
| :--- | :--- |
| Operations reference raw positions, transformed on arrival | Operations reference stable, permanent identifiers |
| Needs a server to establish canonical order | Converges correctly with no central arbiter |
| Transform functions are complex to get right | Higher per-character metadata overhead |

#### Two concurrent edits, transformed to converge

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Client A
  participant S as Edit Server
  participant B as Client B
  A->>S: insert "x" at pos 12
  B->>S: delete at pos 12
  S->>S: transform ops against each other
  S->>A: broadcast resolved delete
  S->>B: broadcast resolved insert
  Note over A,B: both clients converge
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `WS` | `/api/documents/{docId}/connect` | Opens a persistent WebSocket connection for a client editing this document; the server pushes every other editor's operations down this connection and receives this client's operations on it. |
| `POST` | `/api/documents/{docId}/operations` | Body: { base_version, ops: [...] }. Fallback/initial-sync path for a client to submit a batch of local operations relative to the document version it last saw; used on reconnect after an offline period. |
| `GET` | `/api/documents/{docId}/snapshot` | Returns the current full document content plus its version identifier, used when a client first opens the document or needs to resync from scratch. |
| `GET` | `/api/documents/{docId}/history` | Params: before_version. Returns a paginated list of past document snapshots/versions for viewing or restoring history. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `documents`
- `doc_id (unique)`
- `owner_id`
- `current_version (monotonically increasing)`
- `title, created_at, updated_at`
*Notes:* The document row itself doesn't store live content inline for large docs; content is reconstructed from the operation log plus periodic snapshots.

### Entity: `operations`
- `op_id (unique, includes originating client/replica id)`
- `doc_id (indexed)`
- `type (insert | delete | format)`
- `position_or_identifier (a stable position reference, not a raw character index, see deep dive)`
- `content, author_id, applied_at`
*Notes:* Append-only log of every edit ever made to the document; this log is both the real-time sync mechanism and the source of full edit history.

### Entity: `snapshots`
- `doc_id (indexed)`
- `version`
- `full_content`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* Periodic materialized full-document state (e.g. every N operations or every few minutes) so reconstructing current content, or restoring an old version, doesn't require replaying the entire operation log from the beginning every time.

### Entity: `active_sessions (in-memory, not persisted)`
- `doc_id`
- `client_id`
- `connection_reference (which server/socket holds this client's live connection)`
*Notes:* Tracks who is currently connected to which document on which server instance, used to route broadcast messages to the right WebSocket connections.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Operational Transformation vs CRDTs: two different answers to 'how do concurrent edits converge'
Operational Transformation (OT) keeps operations as edits against raw character positions (insert 'x' at index 12), and when two operations happen concurrently, the server transforms the second operation's position to account for the first one already having been applied (if someone inserted 3 characters before index 12, a concurrent delete at index 12 needs to become a delete at index 15). This requires a central server to serialize and transform operations in a specific order. CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) instead give every character a stable, unique, immutable identifier (not a raw index) tied to its logical position relative to its neighbors, so two clients can apply operations in any order, even fully peer-to-peer with no server arbitration, and still converge, because the merge rule is a pure mathematical function of the identifiers, not of arrival order.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- OT: earlier, better-understood in production (this is what Google Docs itself historically used), but the transform functions are notoriously easy to get subtly wrong for complex operation types, and it generally needs a central server to establish a canonical operation order
- CRDTs: converge correctly with no central coordinator at all, which also makes true peer-to-peer and offline-first editing much more natural, but per-character unique identifiers add real memory and bandwidth overhead compared to OT's raw indices, especially for documents with heavy insert/delete churn
- Modern products increasingly lean CRDT (Notion's block model has CRDT-like properties) specifically because it makes offline editing and merge-on-reconnect fall out of the algorithm for free, rather than needing to be bolted on as a special case the way OT reconciliation after a long offline period does

### Why position must be a stable logical identifier, not a raw character index
If operations referenced plain integer positions ('insert at index 50'), then the moment any other operation inserts or deletes text before index 50, every subsequent operation still in flight or offline becomes wrong the instant it's applied, since index 50 in the sender's document no longer means the same character position in the receiver's current document. Both OT (via server-side transformation) and CRDTs (via permanent per-character identifiers, like a fractional index between neighboring characters) exist specifically to solve this: an operation must be expressible in a way that stays meaningful even after the document has changed underneath it.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Raw index-based positions: simple and compact, but only correct if there is zero concurrency, which defeats the entire point of a collaborative editor
- Server-side transformation of index-based operations (OT): keeps the wire format simple, but pushes real algorithmic complexity and correctness risk onto the server's transform logic, and it doesn't tolerate arbitrarily long offline periods well
- Permanent per-character logical identifiers (CRDT): each identifier stays valid forever regardless of what else happens to the document, which is exactly what makes long offline edits and later merges safe, at the cost of every character carrying more metadata than a plain index would

### Real-time propagation architecture: how an edit gets from one client to N others in under a second
Each open document maintains a set of live WebSocket connections, one per active editor, held on whichever application server that client happened to connect to. When server A receives an operation from a client, it needs to get that operation to clients connected to servers B and C as well, not just its own local connections. This requires a pub/sub layer (or a lightweight message bus) that every app server subscribes to per active document, so an operation received on any server gets broadcast to every server hosting a connection for that document, which then pushes it down the relevant WebSocket.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- A shared pub/sub broker (e.g. Redis pub/sub or a message queue) that all app servers subscribe to per-document: decouples app servers from each other, scales naturally as documents and servers are added, but adds one more hop of latency and one more moving piece to keep highly available
- Sticky-session routing so every editor of a given document always connects to the same app server: eliminates the need for cross-server pub/sub entirely for that document, but breaks down the moment a document has enough concurrent editors, or enough total documents, that they can't all fit on one server, and complicates rebalancing when a server needs to drain
- In practice, a hybrid: route by document to a small set of servers when possible for locality, backed by pub/sub for the cases where a document's editors are spread across more servers than that

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single wildly popular, heavily co-edited document (a company-wide live doc with hundreds of simultaneous editors) can concentrate far more WebSocket connections and operation throughput on one document's pub/sub channel than the typical 2 to 5 editor case, and needs the broadcast layer to handle that skew gracefully rather than assuming small fan-out everywhere.
- The operation log for a very long-lived, heavily edited document can grow large; periodic snapshotting bounds how much history needs replaying to reconstruct current state or to catch a client back up after a long offline period.
- Millions of idle-but-open WebSocket connections consume server memory even when no one is typing, so connection-holding capacity per server, not CPU for transform logic, is often the actual horizontal scaling constraint.
- Cross-region latency matters for a genuinely real-time feel; a document's editing session may need to be anchored to servers near where most of its active editors actually are, rather than a single global region for every document.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Designing the sync protocol around raw character indices== and only discovering during a walkthrough that any concurrent edit from another user immediately corrupts every other client's pending operations.
- ⚠️ Treating this as a simple 'broadcast every keystroke to everyone' problem and skipping the actual conflict-resolution algorithm, which is the entire point of the interview question.
- ⚠️ Forgetting offline editing entirely, or hand-waving 'it'll just resync,' without explaining how out-of-order and delayed operations actually merge correctly.
- ⚠️ Not addressing how an edit made on one app server reaches clients connected to a different app server, which silently assumes every collaborator always connects to the same server.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't two clients just send raw character-index-based edits directly to each other and expect the documents to converge?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a character index is only valid relative to the document state the sender was looking at when they made the edit. The instant a concurrent edit changes the document (an insertion or deletion before that index), the same index now refers to a different position in every other client's current document. Convergence requires either transforming operations against everything that happened concurrently (OT) or referencing positions that stay valid forever regardless of concurrent changes (CRDT's stable per-character identifiers). Without one of these, concurrent edits corrupt the document rather than merging into it.

**Q: How does this design keep a user's own typing feeling instant despite going through a server for conflict resolution?**

> **Model Answer:** The client applies its own edit to its local document model immediately, before the round trip to the server even completes, so what the user sees never waits on the network. The edit is sent to the server in the background, transformed/merged against whatever else happened concurrently, and the server's resolved version is what eventually gets broadcast back out (including to the original author, who reconciles it against what they already displayed locally). This local-first application is standard in both OT and CRDT-based editors.

**Q: Why would a system choose CRDTs over OT for a product that needs to support long offline editing sessions?**

> **Model Answer:** OT's transform functions are generally designed assuming operations are reconciled against a relatively recent, mostly-consistent server state; reconciling an edit that's been offline for hours against a huge number of intervening operations gets complex and error-prone. CRDTs assign permanent, stable identifiers to content at creation time, so an operation made offline hours ago is still perfectly well-defined and mergeable whenever it eventually arrives, no matter how much else changed in the meantime, because the merge rule doesn't depend on arrival order at all.

lesson.content:
# Design a Calendar & Scheduling System

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Google Calendar • Calendly` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A recurring meeting that repeats weekly for the next 10 years is not 520 rows waiting to be written, it's **one row and a rule**, and the entire design hinges on computing occurrences on demand from that rule instead of ever materializing the infinite future.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a calendar system: users create events (one-off and recurring),
invite other users, and can view a merged calendar of their own and
others' events. Support looking up when a set of people is free or busy,
across time zones, with invite and RSVP notifications. Design the system
end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How far into the future do we need to support recurring events, and do individual occurrences ever need per-instance edits (like moving just one meeting in a weekly series)?
*Why it matters:* If recurring events are truly infinite (no end date) and any single occurrence can be individually modified or cancelled, the storage model needs to represent both a compact repeating rule and a sparse set of per-instance exceptions layered on top of it, which is significantly more than storing a start/end/repeat flag.

#### Q: Do free/busy lookups need to work across an entire organization (thousands of calendars) for scheduling-assistant-style features, or just for a small, known set of invitees on one event?
*Why it matters:* Checking free/busy for two people invited to one meeting is a cheap, targeted query. Powering a 'find a time that works for these 50 people' or org-wide room-booking feature is a much heavier aggregate query problem that changes how availability data needs to be indexed and cached.

#### Q: How should time zones be handled: is an event's time fixed to a wall-clock time in its creator's zone, or fixed to a specific instant (UTC) regardless of viewer?
*Why it matters:* A recurring '9am standup' should probably still be 9am if the organizer's location observes a daylight-saving shift, meaning it must be stored relative to a time zone and re-resolved, not stored as a fixed UTC instant, which behaves differently (and wrongly, for that use case) across a DST transition.

#### Q: Do we need real-time notification delivery for invites/RSVPs/updates (push within seconds), or is periodic email/digest delivery acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Real-time in-app notification requires a live delivery path (push/WebSocket), while email digests can be handled by a much simpler periodic batch job. This changes whether a notification fan-out service is even part of the critical path.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can create a one-off event or a recurring event (daily, weekly, monthly, or a custom recurrence rule) with a title, time, and location.
- A user can invite other users to an event; invitees can accept, decline, or tentatively RSVP, and see updates when the event changes.
- A user can view a merged calendar of their own events plus any calendars shared with them, in their local time zone.
- The system can answer 'is this person/room free during this time window' for a given set of calendars.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Recurring events must not require storing an unbounded number of rows; storage must stay proportional to the number of recurrence rules, not the number of future occurrences.**
- **Free/busy lookups must be fast (well under a second) even when checking availability across dozens of calendars for a scheduling request.**
- **Event times must render correctly for viewers in different time zones, including correctly across daylight-saving transitions for recurring events.**
- **The system should tolerate eventual consistency for notification delivery (an RSVP update arriving a few seconds late is acceptable) in exchange for a simpler, more available write path.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 300 million users, each averaging 8 active events on their calendar at any time (mix of one-off and recurring series)
- 10% of events are recurring series, the other 90% are one-off events
- An average user checks their calendar 10 times a day and creates or edits an event twice a week
- Average event has 4 invitees

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Total stored event rows (rules, not materialized occurrences):** 300,000,000 users * 8 events ≈ 2.4 billion event rows; since recurring events are stored as one rule regardless of how many future occurrences they represent, this number does not grow with time, only with new events created
- **Occurrences avoided by not materializing:** A weekly recurring event with no end date, viewed over just a 5-year calendar window, represents 260 occurrences; materializing that eagerly for the 10% of events that recur (240 million series) would mean 240,000,000 * 260 ≈ 62 billion extra rows just for a 5-year window, versus the 240 million rule-rows actually needed, a roughly 260x storage blowup avoided
- **Calendar view reads per day:** 300,000,000 * 10 = 3 billion calendar-view reads/day ≈ 35,000 reads/sec average, each needing to expand any recurring rules that overlap the requested date range on the fly
- **RSVP/notification writes per day:** 300,000,000 users / 7 * 2 edits/week ≈ 85 million event edits/week ≈ 12 million/day; each touching ~4 invitees for notification fan-out ≈ 48 million notification events/day, a modest write load compared to the 3 billion daily reads

*Capacity Takeaway:* The single fact driving this architecture is that recurrence rules must be **expanded into concrete occurrences at read time**, on demand, for only the date range being viewed, never stored as individual future rows; skipping this is the difference between 2.4 billion rows and tens of billions, and it's what makes both storage and edit operations (like changing a series) tractable.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Creating a recurring event writes exactly one row containing a recurrence
rule, never individual future occurrences. When a client requests a
calendar view for a date range, the calendar service fetches the relevant
event rules (both one-off events in range and recurring rules that could
produce an occurrence in range), expands each recurring rule into concrete
occurrences for just that window using a recurrence-expansion library,
applies any per-instance exceptions on top, and merges everything into the
final view. Free/busy queries read from a precomputed freebusy_cache
(invalidated and recomputed whenever a user's events change) rather than
expanding rules live, since that path needs to answer quickly across many
calendars at once. Invite creation and RSVP changes go through a
notification service that fans out updates asynchronously to organizer and
invitees, decoupled from the write path itself.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Calendar read path: rule expansion and free/busy cache

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    calsvc["Calendar Service"]:::server
    eventdb[("Events + Exceptions DB")]:::db
    fbcache["Free/Busy Cache"]:::cache
    notifq>"Notification Queue"]:::queue
    notifworker["Notification Workers"]:::server
    client --> lb
    lb --> calsvc
    calsvc -->|"fetch rules + exceptions"| eventdb
    calsvc -->|"read/write busy blocks"| fbcache
    calsvc -.->|"event changed"| notifq
    notifq -.-> notifworker
    notifworker -.->|"push/email invite update"| client
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/events` | Body: { title, start, end, timezone, recurrence_rule?, invitee_ids }. Creates a one-off or recurring event; recurrence_rule follows an RFC 5545 (iCalendar RRULE)-style format. |
| `GET` | `/api/calendars/{userId}/events` | Params: range_start, range_end. Returns all concrete event occurrences (including expanded recurring instances) for the user within the given date range. |
| `PATCH` | `/api/events/{eventId}/instances/{instanceDate}` | Body: { start?, end?, cancelled? }. Modifies or cancels a single occurrence of a recurring series without affecting the rest of the series, creating an exception record. |
| `POST` | `/api/events/{eventId}/rsvp` | Body: { status: accepted|declined|tentative }. Records the authenticated user's response to an invite and triggers a notification to the organizer. |
| `GET` | `/api/freebusy` | Params: user_ids, range_start, range_end. Returns busy time blocks (no event details, just free/busy) for the given set of calendars in the given window. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `events`
- `event_id (unique)`
- `organizer_id`
- `title, location`
- `start_time, end_time, timezone`
- `recurrence_rule (nullable, e.g. FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO;UNTIL=2030-01-01, null for one-off events)`
*Notes:* The single source of truth for a series; recurring events store exactly one row regardless of how many occurrences they'll ever produce.

### Entity: `event_exceptions`
- `event_id (indexed)`
- `original_occurrence_date`
- `modified_start, modified_end (nullable)`
- `cancelled (bool)`
*Notes:* Sparse overrides for individual occurrences of a recurring series (moved, cancelled, or otherwise modified instances), layered on top of the base recurrence rule during expansion; a series with no exceptions has zero rows here.

### Entity: `invitees`
- `event_id (indexed)`
- `user_id (indexed)`
- `rsvp_status (pending | accepted | declined | tentative)`
- `responded_at`
*Notes:* Indexed both by event_id (who's invited to this event) and by user_id (which events is this person invited to, needed for calendar view and free/busy).

### Entity: `freebusy_cache`
- `user_id (key)`
- `date_bucket`
- `busy_intervals (precomputed list of time ranges)`
*Notes:* A denormalized, precomputed cache of busy blocks per user per day, refreshed whenever that user's events change, so free/busy queries across many calendars don't need to expand recurrence rules live on every lookup.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Storing a recurrence rule versus materializing occurrences
Storing a recurrence rule (frequency, interval, days of week, end condition) and expanding it into concrete occurrences only when a specific date range is queried keeps storage bounded and makes editing 'the whole series' trivial (change one row). The cost is that every calendar-view read now has to do real computation: parse the rule and generate every occurrence that falls in the requested window, correctly handling edge cases like 'the last weekday of the month' or a monthly recurrence on the 31st in a month that doesn't have one.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Store-and-expand-on-read: storage stays proportional to the number of series, not occurrences, and editing an entire series is a single-row update, but every read pays an expansion cost, though this is cheap CPU work, not an I/O cost, and is easily cached
- Eager materialization (writing every future occurrence as its own row up front, or in rolling windows): reads become trivial row scans, but writes get vastly more expensive and unbounded (what does 'no end date' even mean for eager materialization), and editing a whole series means rewriting potentially thousands of rows
- A common middle ground: expand on read but cache the expanded result for commonly-viewed near-term windows (e.g. the next 90 days), refreshing the cache only when the underlying rule or an exception changes, getting most of the read-speed benefit of materialization without its storage and edit cost

### Per-instance exceptions: editing or cancelling a single occurrence of a recurring series
A user drags one instance of a weekly recurring meeting to a different time without affecting the rest of the series. This can't be expressed by modifying the base recurrence rule (that would move every occurrence), so it needs a separate sparse exceptions table keyed by the series and the specific occurrence's original date, recording either a modified time or a cancellation. When expanding the rule for a date range, the expansion logic generates the normal occurrences and then applies any matching exceptions on top, skipping or overriding them.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Sparse exception records layered on top of rule expansion: keeps the common case (no exceptions) essentially free, and only pays extra storage/computation for series that actually have modified instances, which in practice is a small minority
- Alternative: 'break' the series into a new standalone event the moment any single instance is edited, keeping the rest as the original rule. This avoids a separate exceptions concept entirely but complicates 'edit the whole series going forward' operations, which now need to know about every split-off fragment
- Google Calendar's actual approach (a canonical rule plus per-instance exception overrides) is the sparse-exception model specifically because most edits to recurring events are one-off tweaks to a single occurrence, not changes to the whole series

### Time zone storage: wall-clock-relative versus fixed UTC instant
A recurring 9am standup should stay at 9am local time for its attendees even when the organizer's region shifts for daylight saving, which means the event must be stored as a wall-clock time plus a time zone identifier (e.g. '09:00 America/New_York'), re-resolved to an absolute instant at render/expansion time using the current DST rules for that zone, rather than stored as a fixed UTC timestamp computed once at creation. A one-off event with a truly fixed instant (like a global product launch announced for a specific UTC second) is the opposite case and should be stored as UTC directly.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Wall-clock + timezone storage (re-resolved at read time): correctly keeps recurring local-time meetings at the intended local time across DST transitions, but requires re-resolving to an absolute instant on every read using up-to-date DST rules, and DST rules themselves occasionally change (a government changes its policy), requiring a timezone-database update
- Fixed UTC instant stored once: simple and requires no re-resolution, but is wrong for the common recurring-local-meeting case, since a fixed UTC time silently drifts by an hour relative to local wall-clock time across a DST boundary
- The correct default is workload-dependent: recurring events default to wall-clock + timezone, one-off events tied to a specific global instant default to fixed UTC, and the system needs to support both rather than picking one universally

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Calendar-view reads dominate write volume roughly 3 billion to 12 million (250:1 in the estimation above); the read path (rule fetch plus expansion) needs aggressive caching for common near-term date ranges, since expansion, while cheap per-call, adds up at this read volume.
- Free/busy queries across large invitee lists (scheduling-assistant features checking dozens of calendars) don't scale well if they have to expand recurrence rules live for every calendar on every query; the precomputed freebusy_cache, invalidated incrementally on event changes, is what keeps this fast.
- A very large organization's shared calendars (an all-hands invite to 50,000 people) creates a notification and RSVP fan-out spike similar to a social-feed celebrity post; this needs async, queue-based fan-out rather than synchronous notification delivery on the write path.
- Recurrence rule expansion logic is a correctness-critical shared library (every service touching calendar data needs identical results for the same rule); it should be a single well-tested component, not reimplemented per service, since subtle bugs (leap years, DST edge cases, 'the 5th Tuesday that doesn't exist this month') are easy to get wrong independently in multiple places.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Materializing every future occurrence== of a recurring event as its own row at creation time, which either caps 'no end date' arbitrarily or grows storage without bound.
- ⚠️ ==Storing all event times as fixed UTC instants==, which silently breaks recurring local-time meetings across daylight-saving transitions.
- ⚠️ Treating a single-occurrence edit to a recurring series the same as editing the whole series, with no concept of a per-instance exception.
- ⚠️ Designing free/busy lookups to expand recurrence rules live for every calendar on every request, which doesn't hold up once a query spans dozens of calendars at once.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: How would you store a weekly meeting that recurs forever, and how do you answer 'what does my calendar look like next March'?**

> **Model Answer:** Store it as a single row: a recurrence rule (e.g. weekly on Tuesdays, no end date) rather than individual future rows. When a client requests any date range, including next March, the calendar service expands the rule on the fly, generating only the occurrences that fall within the requested window, and merges in any per-instance exceptions for that series. Storage never grows just because time passes or the rule has no end date, since nothing is materialized until a read actually asks for a specific range.

**Q: A user drags a single instance of a recurring meeting to a different time. How does that not affect the rest of the series?**

> **Model Answer:** The base recurrence rule stays untouched. The system writes a row to a separate exceptions table, keyed by the series' event_id and that occurrence's original date, recording the new time (or a cancellation). When the rule is expanded for a date range that includes that occurrence, the expansion logic checks for a matching exception and applies the override instead of the rule-generated default, while every other occurrence in the series is generated normally, unaffected.

**Q: Why can't a recurring 9am meeting just be stored as a fixed UTC timestamp plus 'repeat every 7 days'?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a fixed UTC timestamp represents one specific instant, and adding 7 days to a UTC instant is not the same as 'stay at 9am local time' across a daylight-saving transition; the wall-clock time would drift by an hour relative to what attendees actually expect. Storing the event as a wall-clock time (09:00) plus a time zone identifier, and resolving it to an absolute instant using that time zone's current DST rules whenever it's expanded or displayed, is what keeps the meeting correctly at 9am local time year-round.

# Design a Calendar & Scheduling System

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Google Calendar • Calendly` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A recurring meeting that repeats weekly for the next 10 years is not 520 rows waiting to be written, it's **one row and a rule**, and the entire design hinges on computing occurrences on demand from that rule instead of ever materializing the infinite future.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a calendar system: users create events (one-off and recurring),
invite other users, and can view a merged calendar of their own and
others' events. Support looking up when a set of people is free or busy,
across time zones, with invite and RSVP notifications. Design the system
end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How far into the future do we need to support recurring events, and do individual occurrences ever need per-instance edits (like moving just one meeting in a weekly series)?
*Why it matters:* If recurring events are truly infinite (no end date) and any single occurrence can be individually modified or cancelled, the storage model needs to represent both a compact repeating rule and a sparse set of per-instance exceptions layered on top of it, which is significantly more than storing a start/end/repeat flag.

#### Q: Do free/busy lookups need to work across an entire organization (thousands of calendars) for scheduling-assistant-style features, or just for a small, known set of invitees on one event?
*Why it matters:* Checking free/busy for two people invited to one meeting is a cheap, targeted query. Powering a 'find a time that works for these 50 people' or org-wide room-booking feature is a much heavier aggregate query problem that changes how availability data needs to be indexed and cached.

#### Q: How should time zones be handled: is an event's time fixed to a wall-clock time in its creator's zone, or fixed to a specific instant (UTC) regardless of viewer?
*Why it matters:* A recurring '9am standup' should probably still be 9am if the organizer's location observes a daylight-saving shift, meaning it must be stored relative to a time zone and re-resolved, not stored as a fixed UTC instant, which behaves differently (and wrongly, for that use case) across a DST transition.

#### Q: Do we need real-time notification delivery for invites/RSVPs/updates (push within seconds), or is periodic email/digest delivery acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Real-time in-app notification requires a live delivery path (push/WebSocket), while email digests can be handled by a much simpler periodic batch job. This changes whether a notification fan-out service is even part of the critical path.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can create a one-off event or a recurring event (daily, weekly, monthly, or a custom recurrence rule) with a title, time, and location.
- A user can invite other users to an event; invitees can accept, decline, or tentatively RSVP, and see updates when the event changes.
- A user can view a merged calendar of their own events plus any calendars shared with them, in their local time zone.
- The system can answer 'is this person/room free during this time window' for a given set of calendars.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Recurring events must not require storing an unbounded number of rows; storage must stay proportional to the number of recurrence rules, not the number of future occurrences.**
- **Free/busy lookups must be fast (well under a second) even when checking availability across dozens of calendars for a scheduling request.**
- **Event times must render correctly for viewers in different time zones, including correctly across daylight-saving transitions for recurring events.**
- **The system should tolerate eventual consistency for notification delivery (an RSVP update arriving a few seconds late is acceptable) in exchange for a simpler, more available write path.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 300 million users, each averaging 8 active events on their calendar at any time (mix of one-off and recurring series)
- 10% of events are recurring series, the other 90% are one-off events
- An average user checks their calendar 10 times a day and creates or edits an event twice a week
- Average event has 4 invitees

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Total stored event rows (rules, not materialized occurrences):** 300,000,000 users * 8 events ≈ 2.4 billion event rows; since recurring events are stored as one rule regardless of how many future occurrences they represent, this number does not grow with time, only with new events created
- **Occurrences avoided by not materializing:** A weekly recurring event with no end date, viewed over just a 5-year calendar window, represents 260 occurrences; materializing that eagerly for the 10% of events that recur (240 million series) would mean 240,000,000 * 260 ≈ 62 billion extra rows just for a 5-year window, versus the 240 million rule-rows actually needed, a roughly 260x storage blowup avoided
- **Calendar view reads per day:** 300,000,000 * 10 = 3 billion calendar-view reads/day ≈ 35,000 reads/sec average, each needing to expand any recurring rules that overlap the requested date range on the fly
- **RSVP/notification writes per day:** 300,000,000 users / 7 * 2 edits/week ≈ 85 million event edits/week ≈ 12 million/day; each touching ~4 invitees for notification fan-out ≈ 48 million notification events/day, a modest write load compared to the 3 billion daily reads

*Capacity Takeaway:* The single fact driving this architecture is that recurrence rules must be **expanded into concrete occurrences at read time**, on demand, for only the date range being viewed, never stored as individual future rows; skipping this is the difference between 2.4 billion rows and tens of billions, and it's what makes both storage and edit operations (like changing a series) tractable.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Creating a recurring event writes exactly one row containing a recurrence
rule, never individual future occurrences. When a client requests a
calendar view for a date range, the calendar service fetches the relevant
event rules (both one-off events in range and recurring rules that could
produce an occurrence in range), expands each recurring rule into concrete
occurrences for just that window using a recurrence-expansion library,
applies any per-instance exceptions on top, and merges everything into the
final view. Free/busy queries read from a precomputed freebusy_cache
(invalidated and recomputed whenever a user's events change) rather than
expanding rules live, since that path needs to answer quickly across many
calendars at once. Invite creation and RSVP changes go through a
notification service that fans out updates asynchronously to organizer and
invitees, decoupled from the write path itself.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Calendar read path: rule expansion and free/busy cache

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    calsvc["Calendar Service"]:::server
    eventdb[("Events + Exceptions DB")]:::db
    fbcache["Free/Busy Cache"]:::cache
    notifq>"Notification Queue"]:::queue
    notifworker["Notification Workers"]:::server
    client --> lb
    lb --> calsvc
    calsvc -->|"fetch rules + exceptions"| eventdb
    calsvc -->|"read/write busy blocks"| fbcache
    calsvc -.->|"event changed"| notifq
    notifq -.-> notifworker
    notifworker -.->|"push/email invite update"| client
```

#### Requesting a calendar view for a date range

#### Stored rows: rule-based vs eager materialization

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/events` | Body: { title, start, end, timezone, recurrence_rule?, invitee_ids }. Creates a one-off or recurring event; recurrence_rule follows an RFC 5545 (iCalendar RRULE)-style format. |
| `GET` | `/api/calendars/{userId}/events` | Params: range_start, range_end. Returns all concrete event occurrences (including expanded recurring instances) for the user within the given date range. |
| `PATCH` | `/api/events/{eventId}/instances/{instanceDate}` | Body: { start?, end?, cancelled? }. Modifies or cancels a single occurrence of a recurring series without affecting the rest of the series, creating an exception record. |
| `POST` | `/api/events/{eventId}/rsvp` | Body: { status: accepted|declined|tentative }. Records the authenticated user's response to an invite and triggers a notification to the organizer. |
| `GET` | `/api/freebusy` | Params: user_ids, range_start, range_end. Returns busy time blocks (no event details, just free/busy) for the given set of calendars in the given window. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `events`
- `event_id (unique)`
- `organizer_id`
- `title, location`
- `start_time, end_time, timezone`
- `recurrence_rule (nullable, e.g. FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO;UNTIL=2030-01-01, null for one-off events)`
*Notes:* The single source of truth for a series; recurring events store exactly one row regardless of how many occurrences they'll ever produce.

### Entity: `event_exceptions`
- `event_id (indexed)`
- `original_occurrence_date`
- `modified_start, modified_end (nullable)`
- `cancelled (bool)`
*Notes:* Sparse overrides for individual occurrences of a recurring series (moved, cancelled, or otherwise modified instances), layered on top of the base recurrence rule during expansion; a series with no exceptions has zero rows here.

### Entity: `invitees`
- `event_id (indexed)`
- `user_id (indexed)`
- `rsvp_status (pending | accepted | declined | tentative)`
- `responded_at`
*Notes:* Indexed both by event_id (who's invited to this event) and by user_id (which events is this person invited to, needed for calendar view and free/busy).

### Entity: `freebusy_cache`
- `user_id (key)`
- `date_bucket`
- `busy_intervals (precomputed list of time ranges)`
*Notes:* A denormalized, precomputed cache of busy blocks per user per day, refreshed whenever that user's events change, so free/busy queries across many calendars don't need to expand recurrence rules live on every lookup.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Storing a recurrence rule versus materializing occurrences
Storing a recurrence rule (frequency, interval, days of week, end condition) and expanding it into concrete occurrences only when a specific date range is queried keeps storage bounded and makes editing 'the whole series' trivial (change one row). The cost is that every calendar-view read now has to do real computation: parse the rule and generate every occurrence that falls in the requested window, correctly handling edge cases like 'the last weekday of the month' or a monthly recurrence on the 31st in a month that doesn't have one.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Store-and-expand-on-read: storage stays proportional to the number of series, not occurrences, and editing an entire series is a single-row update, but every read pays an expansion cost, though this is cheap CPU work, not an I/O cost, and is easily cached
- Eager materialization (writing every future occurrence as its own row up front, or in rolling windows): reads become trivial row scans, but writes get vastly more expensive and unbounded (what does 'no end date' even mean for eager materialization), and editing a whole series means rewriting potentially thousands of rows
- A common middle ground: expand on read but cache the expanded result for commonly-viewed near-term windows (e.g. the next 90 days), refreshing the cache only when the underlying rule or an exception changes, getting most of the read-speed benefit of materialization without its storage and edit cost

### Per-instance exceptions: editing or cancelling a single occurrence of a recurring series
A user drags one instance of a weekly recurring meeting to a different time without affecting the rest of the series. This can't be expressed by modifying the base recurrence rule (that would move every occurrence), so it needs a separate sparse exceptions table keyed by the series and the specific occurrence's original date, recording either a modified time or a cancellation. When expanding the rule for a date range, the expansion logic generates the normal occurrences and then applies any matching exceptions on top, skipping or overriding them.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Sparse exception records layered on top of rule expansion: keeps the common case (no exceptions) essentially free, and only pays extra storage/computation for series that actually have modified instances, which in practice is a small minority
- Alternative: 'break' the series into a new standalone event the moment any single instance is edited, keeping the rest as the original rule. This avoids a separate exceptions concept entirely but complicates 'edit the whole series going forward' operations, which now need to know about every split-off fragment
- Google Calendar's actual approach (a canonical rule plus per-instance exception overrides) is the sparse-exception model specifically because most edits to recurring events are one-off tweaks to a single occurrence, not changes to the whole series

### Time zone storage: wall-clock-relative versus fixed UTC instant
A recurring 9am standup should stay at 9am local time for its attendees even when the organizer's region shifts for daylight saving, which means the event must be stored as a wall-clock time plus a time zone identifier (e.g. '09:00 America/New_York'), re-resolved to an absolute instant at render/expansion time using the current DST rules for that zone, rather than stored as a fixed UTC timestamp computed once at creation. A one-off event with a truly fixed instant (like a global product launch announced for a specific UTC second) is the opposite case and should be stored as UTC directly.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Wall-clock + timezone storage (re-resolved at read time): correctly keeps recurring local-time meetings at the intended local time across DST transitions, but requires re-resolving to an absolute instant on every read using up-to-date DST rules, and DST rules themselves occasionally change (a government changes its policy), requiring a timezone-database update
- Fixed UTC instant stored once: simple and requires no re-resolution, but is wrong for the common recurring-local-meeting case, since a fixed UTC time silently drifts by an hour relative to local wall-clock time across a DST boundary
- The correct default is workload-dependent: recurring events default to wall-clock + timezone, one-off events tied to a specific global instant default to fixed UTC, and the system needs to support both rather than picking one universally

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Calendar-view reads dominate write volume roughly 3 billion to 12 million (250:1 in the estimation above); the read path (rule fetch plus expansion) needs aggressive caching for common near-term date ranges, since expansion, while cheap per-call, adds up at this read volume.
- Free/busy queries across large invitee lists (scheduling-assistant features checking dozens of calendars) don't scale well if they have to expand recurrence rules live for every calendar on every query; the precomputed freebusy_cache, invalidated incrementally on event changes, is what keeps this fast.
- A very large organization's shared calendars (an all-hands invite to 50,000 people) creates a notification and RSVP fan-out spike similar to a social-feed celebrity post; this needs async, queue-based fan-out rather than synchronous notification delivery on the write path.
- Recurrence rule expansion logic is a correctness-critical shared library (every service touching calendar data needs identical results for the same rule); it should be a single well-tested component, not reimplemented per service, since subtle bugs (leap years, DST edge cases, 'the 5th Tuesday that doesn't exist this month') are easy to get wrong independently in multiple places.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Materializing every future occurrence== of a recurring event as its own row at creation time, which either caps 'no end date' arbitrarily or grows storage without bound.
- ⚠️ ==Storing all event times as fixed UTC instants==, which silently breaks recurring local-time meetings across daylight-saving transitions.
- ⚠️ Treating a single-occurrence edit to a recurring series the same as editing the whole series, with no concept of a per-instance exception.
- ⚠️ Designing free/busy lookups to expand recurrence rules live for every calendar on every request, which doesn't hold up once a query spans dozens of calendars at once.

> **Model Answer:** Store it as a single row: a recurrence rule (e.g. weekly on Tuesdays, no end date) rather than individual future rows. lesson.content:
# Design a Task Management Tool (Trello/Jira)

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Trello • Jira • Asana` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The genuinely hard part isn't the board/list/card hierarchy, it's that dragging one card between two others must produce a stable, low-conflict **ordering value** without ever having to renumber every other card on the board, because ==renumbering is exactly the operation that makes concurrent drags collide==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a task management tool: workspaces contain boards, boards contain
lists (columns), lists contain cards. Users can create, move, and edit
cards, including dragging a card between lists or reordering it within a
list, and multiple people viewing the same board should see changes live.
Support an activity history and search/filter across a large workspace.
Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How many people typically view or edit one board concurrently, and does the product need Google-Docs-style character-level merge, or is card-level granularity enough?
*Why it matters:* Task boards are usually edited at the card level (move a whole card, edit a whole field), not character by character within a field simultaneously. This is a much lighter concurrency problem than free-text collaborative editing, and assuming otherwise leads to solving a harder problem than the one that's actually being asked.

#### Q: How large does a single workspace get, thousands of cards or millions, and does search/filter need to work across the whole workspace or just within one board?
*Why it matters:* A single board with a few hundred cards can be served entirely from one query with no special indexing. A workspace with millions of cards across thousands of boards needs a dedicated search index and changes how filtering is implemented, it can't just be a WHERE clause against the primary database at that scale.

#### Q: What exactly needs real-time propagation: card moves and edits, or also lower-priority things like comments and activity feed entries?
*Why it matters:* Card position and core field changes need to feel instant since they're the primary interaction (dragging a card). Comments and activity history are commonly acceptable with a slight delay, which changes what needs a live WebSocket path versus what can be a simple poll or refresh.

#### Q: Does every card change need to be individually auditable (who changed what, when), and for how long must that history be retained?
*Why it matters:* A full audit log changes the write path (every mutation needs to also produce an immutable history entry) and the storage growth profile (history can dwarf the size of current-state data over a workspace's lifetime), so it needs to be planned for, not bolted on later.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can create boards, lists, and cards, and move a card between lists or reorder it within a list, including via drag-and-drop.
- Multiple users viewing the same board see card creates, edits, and moves from other users live, without a manual refresh.
- Every change to a card (field edits, moves, comments) is recorded in an activity history visible on the card and the board.
- A user can search and filter cards across an entire workspace by text, assignee, label, or due date.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Reordering a card within a list or moving it to another list must not require rewriting the position of every other card on the board.**
- **Live updates to an open board should reach other viewers within roughly a second.**
- **The activity history must be append-only and immutable, since it's the audit trail for who changed what.**
- **Search/filter across a large workspace must return results in well under a second, even across millions of cards.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 5 million workspaces, averaging 40 boards each, averaging 60 cards per board
- 10% of workspace members are active on a given day, and an active user performs roughly 30 card actions (create/edit/move/comment) a day
- 500,000 daily active users total across the platform, with an average of 4 concurrent viewers on a board that's actively being used
- Each activity log entry is about 200 bytes

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Total cards stored:** 5,000,000 workspaces * 40 boards * 60 cards = 12 billion cards; even a compact position field per card matters at this row count
- **Card actions per day:** 500,000 active users * 30 actions = 15 million actions/day ≈ 175 writes/sec average, modest, but bursty around business hours
- **Activity log growth per day:** 15,000,000 actions * 200 bytes ≈ 3 GB/day of append-only history, ≈ 1.1 TB/year cluster-wide, which is small enough to keep indefinitely if stored efficiently, unlike current-state card data which stays roughly constant in size
- **Live broadcast fan-out per action:** 15,000,000 actions/day, each broadcast to ~3 other concurrent viewers (4 viewers - 1 actor) on that board = 45 million broadcast messages/day ≈ 520/sec average, trivial volume, the real cost is holding many idle WebSocket connections open, not the message rate itself

*Capacity Takeaway:* The number that shapes this design is 12 billion cards needing a reorderable position, not the moderate write or broadcast rate: at that scale, any operation that has to touch more than the one card being moved (like renumbering neighbors) turns a single drag into a fan-out write against the busiest, most contended part of the schema, which is exactly what a fractional/lexicographic ordering scheme is built to avoid.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Boards, lists, and cards form a simple hierarchy backed by a normal
relational or document store, with each card carrying a fractional
position key that orders it within its list without needing to touch any
other card's row. Dragging a card computes a new position key between its
two intended neighbors client-side (or server-confirmed), and moving a card
to a different list is just an update to its list_id and position, an O(1)
write regardless of board size. Every mutation also appends an immutable
entry to the activity_log, which powers both the card-level history view
and the board-level activity feed. Clients viewing an open board hold a
WebSocket connection to a board-scoped channel; any mutation is broadcast
to other connected viewers so moves and edits appear live. A separate,
asynchronously updated search index serves workspace-wide search and
filtering, since that access pattern doesn't fit the primary store's
per-board query shape.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Card move: write path, live broadcast, and search indexing

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["Board Service"]:::server
    carddb[("Cards/Lists DB")]:::db
    pubsub>"Board Pub/Sub"]:::queue
    otherclients["Other Viewers"]:::client
    outbox>"Change Outbox"]:::queue
    searchidx["Search Index"]:::server
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -->|"update position/list_id"| carddb
    app -.->|"publish card moved"| pubsub
    pubsub -.-> otherclients
    carddb -.->|"change event"| outbox
    outbox -.->|"reindex card"| searchidx
```

#### Dragging a card to a new position

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. User drags card between two neighbors (client identifies target list and neighbor cards)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Client computes new position key (lexicographic key sorting between the neighbors)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Server validates and commits the move (single-row update to list_id and position)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Server appends an activity log entry (immutable, records before/after list and position)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Server publishes the move to the board's channel (async broadcast)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. Other connected viewers apply the move live (no full board reload needed)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
```

#### Should this list rebalance its position keys?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  drag["Card dragged to new spot"] --> gen["Generate key between neighbors"]
  gen --> check{"Key length over threshold?"}
  check -->|"no"| commit["Commit key, done"]
  check -->|"yes"| queue["Queue background rebalance"]
  queue --> commit
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/boards/{boardId}/cards` | Body: { list_id, title, position? }. Creates a new card in the given list; if position is omitted, the card is placed at the end. |
| `PATCH` | `/api/cards/{cardId}/move` | Body: { target_list_id, position_key }. Moves a card to a new list and/or position, where position_key is a precomputed ordering key placing it between two neighbors. |
| `WS` | `/api/boards/{boardId}/connect` | Opens a persistent connection for a client viewing this board; the server pushes card creates/edits/moves from other users made on this board. |
| `GET` | `/api/cards/{cardId}/activity` | Returns the immutable, paginated activity history for a single card. |

### Ordering cards within a list without renumbering: fractional (lexicographic) positions

# Design a Task Management Tool (Trello/Jira)

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Trello • Jira • Asana` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The genuinely hard part isn't the board/list/card hierarchy, it's that dragging one card between two others must produce a stable, low-conflict **ordering value** without ever having to renumber every other card on the board, because ==renumbering is exactly the operation that makes concurrent drags collide==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a task management tool: workspaces contain boards, boards contain
lists (columns), lists contain cards. Users can create, move, and edit
cards, including dragging a card between lists or reordering it within a
list, and multiple people viewing the same board should see changes live.
Support an activity history and search/filter across a large workspace.
Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How many people typically view or edit one board concurrently, and does the product need Google-Docs-style character-level merge, or is card-level granularity enough?
*Why it matters:* Task boards are usually edited at the card level (move a whole card, edit a whole field), not character by character within a field simultaneously. This is a much lighter concurrency problem than free-text collaborative editing, and assuming otherwise leads to solving a harder problem than the one that's actually being asked.

#### Q: How large does a single workspace get, thousands of cards or millions, and does search/filter need to work across the whole workspace or just within one board?
*Why it matters:* A single board with a few hundred cards can be served entirely from one query with no special indexing. A workspace with millions of cards across thousands of boards needs a dedicated search index and changes how filtering is implemented, it can't just be a WHERE clause against the primary database at that scale.

#### Q: What exactly needs real-time propagation: card moves and edits, or also lower-priority things like comments and activity feed entries?
*Why it matters:* Card position and core field changes need to feel instant since they're the primary interaction (dragging a card). Comments and activity history are commonly acceptable with a slight delay, which changes what needs a live WebSocket path versus what can be a simple poll or refresh.

#### Q: Does every card change need to be individually auditable (who changed what, when), and for how long must that history be retained?
*Why it matters:* A full audit log changes the write path (every mutation needs to also produce an immutable history entry) and the storage growth profile (history can dwarf the size of current-state data over a workspace's lifetime), so it needs to be planned for, not bolted on later.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can create boards, lists, and cards, and move a card between lists or reorder it within a list, including via drag-and-drop.
- Multiple users viewing the same board see card creates, edits, and moves from other users live, without a manual refresh.
- Every change to a card (field edits, moves, comments) is recorded in an activity history visible on the card and the board.
- A user can search and filter cards across an entire workspace by text, assignee, label, or due date.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Reordering a card within a list or moving it to another list must not require rewriting the position of every other card on the board.**
- **Live updates to an open board should reach other viewers within roughly a second.**
- **The activity history must be append-only and immutable, since it's the audit trail for who changed what.**
- **Search/filter across a large workspace must return results in well under a second, even across millions of cards.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 5 million workspaces, averaging 40 boards each, averaging 60 cards per board
- 10% of workspace members are active on a given day, and an active user performs roughly 30 card actions (create/edit/move/comment) a day
- 500,000 daily active users total across the platform, with an average of 4 concurrent viewers on a board that's actively being used
- Each activity log entry is about 200 bytes

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Total cards stored:** 5,000,000 workspaces * 40 boards * 60 cards = 12 billion cards; even a compact position field per card matters at this row count
- **Card actions per day:** 500,000 active users * 30 actions = 15 million actions/day ≈ 175 writes/sec average, modest, but bursty around business hours

- **Live broadcast fan-out per action:** 15,000,000 actions/day, each broadcast to ~3 other concurrent viewers (4 viewers - 1 actor) on that board = 45 million broadcast messages/day ≈ 520/sec average, trivial volume, the real cost is holding many idle WebSocket connections open, not the message rate itself

Boards, lists, and cards form a simple hierarchy backed by a normal

#### Card move: write path, live broadcast, and search indexing

    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;

    carddb[("Cards/Lists DB")]:::db
    pubsub>"Board Pub/Sub"]:::queue

    outbox>"Change Outbox"]:::queue
    searchidx["Search Index"]:::server
    client --> lb

    app -.->|"publish card moved"| pubsub

    carddb -.->|"change event"| outbox

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a real-time collaborative whiteboard: multiple users on the same
board can create, move, resize, and restyle shapes (rectangles, text,
sticky notes, freehand strokes) on a large canvas, see each other's cursors
and selections live, and the canvas syncs efficiently without redownloading
the entire board on every small change. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Are we syncing structured objects (shapes with position/size/style properties) or raw pixel/freehand drawing data, or both?
*Why it matters:* Structured objects can be synced as small property-level deltas (x changed from 100 to 140). Freehand pen strokes are effectively an append-only stream of points, a different data shape entirely, and a board mixing both needs to support two different sync representations, not force one into the other.

#### Q: How large does a single board get, tens of objects or tens of thousands, and does a client need the whole board loaded at once or only the visible viewport?
*Why it matters:* A small board can be fully loaded and kept in memory by every client cheaply. A board with tens of thousands of objects makes 'send the whole board on load' expensive and pushes toward viewport-based partial loading and spatial indexing, a materially different client and server architecture.

#### Q: How many concurrent editors does one board typically need to support, a handful or hundreds (like a live workshop)?
*Why it matters:* A handful of concurrent editors keeps cursor/selection broadcast trivially cheap. Supporting hundreds of simultaneous editors on one board (a live brainstorm with a large team) turns cursor broadcast, which is the highest-frequency event in the whole system, into a real fan-out scaling problem on its own.

#### Q: Do offline edits need to merge back in automatically, or is a live connection to the board effectively required to edit it?
*Why it matters:* If offline editing must be supported, object mutations need conflict-free merge semantics (CRDT-style) so a shape moved on two disconnected devices converges predictably. If a live connection is assumed, a simpler server-arbitrated last-write-wins-per-object model can be enough.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can create, move, resize, restyle, and delete shapes and text on a shared canvas, with changes visible to other viewers live.
- Users viewing the same board see each other's live cursor position and current selection.
- The system supports a large canvas efficiently: a client only needs to load and sync objects relevant to what it's currently viewing, not the entire board upfront.
- A board's edit history can be viewed, and the system supports undo/redo per user session.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **A change to one object (move, resize, restyle) must sync to other viewers as a small delta describing just that object's change, not a re-send of the whole board.**
- **Cursor and selection broadcast, the highest-frequency event type in the system, must not degrade the latency of actual object edits.**
- **The system must support boards with tens of thousands of objects without every client having to hold the entire board's full detail in memory at once.**
- **Two users moving two different objects at the same time must both succeed without either edit being lost, since they are not a real conflict.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 2 million daily active boards, averaging 3 concurrent editors during an active session
- An actively-editing user generates roughly 10 object-mutation events per second while actively dragging/resizing (throttled from raw mouse events)
- Cursor position updates are generated far more often, roughly 20 per second per active user, but are ephemeral and not persisted
- Average board has 800 objects; average object's serialized delta is about 150 bytes, a full object record is about 400 bytes

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Concurrent active editing sessions at peak:** 2,000,000 boards * a fraction active concurrently, say 5% at peak = 100,000 concurrently active boards * 3 editors ≈ 300,000 concurrent editors platform-wide at peak
- **Object mutation events per second, cluster-wide:** 300,000 concurrent editors, but only a fraction actively dragging at any instant, say 20% = 60,000 * 10 events/sec ≈ 600,000 object mutation events/sec at peak, each a small delta
- **Cursor broadcast events per second, cluster-wide:** 300,000 concurrent editors * 20 cursor updates/sec = 6,000,000 cursor events/sec, roughly 10x the object-mutation rate, which is why cursor traffic needs to be treated as a separate, lower-priority, droppable stream rather than sharing a path with real object edits

*Capacity Takeaway:* The number that defines this architecture is that ephemeral cursor traffic (6 million events/sec) outweighs real object-mutation traffic (600,000 events/sec) by roughly **10x**, so the system must treat cursor/selection broadcast as a separate, best-effort, non-persisted stream that can be dropped or throttled under load without ever risking the correctness-critical, persisted object-mutation path.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Each object on the board (a shape, sticky note, or text box) has its own
independent position, size, and style, so an edit to one object produces a
small, self-contained delta rather than a change to a shared linear
structure. A client only loads objects intersecting its current viewport,
using a spatial index on the objects table, and pans/zooms trigger
incremental loads of newly visible regions rather than ever fetching the
whole board. Object mutations are sent over a persistent connection,
applied to the objects table, appended to the durable object_mutations log
(which powers history and undo/redo), and broadcast to other viewers on a
board-scoped channel. Cursor and selection updates travel over the same
connection but through a completely separate, ephemeral, non-durable path:
never written to a database, broadcast best-effort, and safe to drop under
load, since losing one cursor update has no lasting consequence while

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
