## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `boards`
- `board_id (unique)`
- `owner_id, title`
- `created_at, updated_at`
*Notes:* Top-level container; permissions and sharing are modeled at this level.

### Entity: `objects`
- `object_id (unique)`
- `board_id (indexed)`
- `type (rectangle | text | sticky_note | freehand_path | ...)`
- `x, y, width, height, rotation`
- `z_index (stacking order)`
- `style_properties, content`
*Notes:* Spatially indexed by (board_id, x, y) so viewport queries can efficiently fetch only objects intersecting a given region rather than scanning the whole board.

### Entity: `object_mutations (append-only)`
- `mutation_id (unique, time-sortable)`
- `object_id, board_id (indexed)`
- `actor_id, changed_properties (the delta, not the full object)`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* Durable log of every real object change, used for board history, undo/redo, and as the durable source of truth that current object state is derived from; deliberately separate from the ephemeral cursor stream, which is never logged here.

### Entity: `presence (in-memory, not persisted)`
- `board_id, user_id`
- `cursor_x, cursor_y, selected_object_ids`
- `last_updated_at`
*Notes:* Live-only state, held in memory (e.g. in the pub/sub layer or a fast in-memory store), expired quickly if a user disconnects; never written to durable storage since a stale cursor position has no lasting value.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Per-object deltas versus whole-document diffing (why this problem is easier than text collaborative editing in one specific way)
In a text document, content is one linear sequence, so even a small edit potentially shifts every character after it, which is why text collaborative editing needs OT or CRDT machinery to resolve position conflicts. A whiteboard object's position, size, and style are independent properties on an independent entity with a stable id; moving object A never changes object B's coordinates. This means two users editing two different objects at the same time aren't in conflict at all, they're just two independent deltas that can both apply directly with no merge logic needed. Conflict only exists when two users mutate the exact same object's same property concurrently, a narrower and easier problem.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Per-object independent deltas: the common case (different users editing different objects) needs zero conflict resolution, which is a materially simpler baseline than a shared linear document's merge problem
- Same-object concurrent edits still need a resolution rule (e.g. last-write-wins per property, using a server-assigned or logical timestamp), which is simple to implement but can silently drop one user's concurrent edit to the very same property of the very same object, an accepted, narrow trade-off given how rare that specific collision is in practice
- A CRDT-based approach per-object (each property change tagged with a version vector, merged rather than overwritten) removes even that narrow last-write-wins loss, at the cost of extra metadata per object and more complex client logic, generally justified only if offline editing with later merge is a hard requirement

### Viewport-based partial sync for a large canvas
Sending an entire board's objects to every client on load doesn't scale once boards have thousands of objects, most of which aren't currently visible to any given viewer. Instead, the server maintains a spatial index (e.g. a grid or quadtree keyed by object position) over the board's objects, and a client requests only the objects intersecting its current viewport bounds. As a user pans or zooms, the client requests the newly-exposed region incrementally rather than reloading the board. Real-time updates for objects outside a client's current viewport can be safely skipped or queued at lower priority, since the client can't see them anyway.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Full board load on open: simplest to implement and means a client always has every object in memory ready for any pan/zoom with no extra round trip, but doesn't scale past a moderate object count, and wastes bandwidth loading objects a user may never scroll to
- Viewport-scoped spatial queries with incremental loading on pan/zoom: scales to very large boards and keeps initial load fast, at the cost of a brief loading flicker when panning into a previously-unloaded region, and real-time updates now need to be filtered per-client by what's in their current viewport rather than blindly broadcast to everyone
- A hybrid used in practice: eagerly load a margin beyond the current viewport (so small pans don't trigger a visible load), and fall back to full-board load transparently for boards under some object-count threshold where the added complexity isn't worth it

### Separating cursor/presence broadcast from object-mutation broadcast
Cursor position updates happen far more frequently than actual object edits (per the capacity math, roughly 10x the event rate) and carry no lasting value, a stale cursor position from half a second ago is simply irrelevant once a newer one arrives, unlike an object mutation which must never be lost. Routing both through the same durable, ordered, at-least-once delivery path would mean the high-frequency, disposable cursor stream competes for the same infrastructure guarantees (durability, ordering, retry) that the low-frequency, correctness-critical object stream actually needs, and under load, that competition risks degrading the path that matters.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- One unified event stream for both cursor and object updates: simpler to build (one channel, one delivery guarantee), but forces the correctness-critical object-mutation path to share capacity and backpressure behavior with 10x the volume of throwaway cursor events
- Two separate paths, ephemeral best-effort for cursor/presence (fine to drop or coalesce under load, often UDP-like or a lightweight non-durable pub/sub) and durable at-least-once for object mutations (persisted, retried, ordered): correctly isolates the two very different reliability needs, at the cost of more moving infrastructure pieces to build and operate
- Coalescing cursor updates (only sending the latest position within a throttle window, e.g. 20 times/sec instead of raw mousemove rate) further cuts the 6 million events/sec figure without any loss of perceived smoothness, since human perception can't distinguish a coalesced 20Hz cursor update from a raw one

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Cursor/presence broadcast volume (roughly 10x object-mutation volume in the estimation above) is the single highest-frequency traffic in the system and must be architecturally isolated (separate ephemeral path, client-side throttling/coalescing) so it can never degrade the durable object-mutation path under load.
- A very large board (tens of thousands of objects) stresses the spatial index and the viewport-query path; the index needs to support efficient range queries as objects move (a moved object's index entry must update), not just efficient lookup of static positions.
- A board with unusually high concurrent editor counts (a large live workshop) multiplies both mutation and cursor broadcast fan-out on that one board; this resembles a hotspot problem and may need that specific board's traffic isolated onto dedicated capacity rather than sharing a general pool sized for the 3-editor average case.
- The object_mutations durable log grows without bound for a long-lived, heavily-edited board; like other append-only history logs, it benefits from time-based partitioning and, for undo/redo (which typically only needs recent history), a bounded recent-window cache separate from full historical storage.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Treating every concurrent edit as a conflict== requiring merge logic, when most concurrent edits are on different objects and need no resolution at all.
- ⚠️ ==Loading and syncing an entire board's objects== on every client, which doesn't scale once boards grow past a modest object count.
- ⚠️ Routing cursor/presence updates through the same durable, ordered delivery path as object mutations, letting a 10x-higher-frequency disposable stream compete with correctness-critical traffic.
- ⚠️ Persisting every cursor position update to a database, which is unnecessary write load for data that's irrelevant the instant a newer update arrives.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is syncing a whiteboard fundamentally easier than syncing a shared text document, even though both are 'real-time collaborative editing'?**

> **Model Answer:** A text document is one linear sequence, so any insertion or deletion can shift the meaning of every subsequent position, which is why concurrent text edits need OT or CRDT machinery to resolve. A whiteboard's objects each have their own independent position, size, and properties tied to a stable id; moving one object has zero effect on any other object's data. That means the common case, two users editing two different objects at the same time, requires no conflict resolution at all, they're just two independent deltas. The only remaining conflict case is two users editing the exact same property of the exact same object concurrently, a much narrower problem that a simple last-write-wins rule handles adequately.

**Q: How would you design sync for a board with 50,000 objects without sending the whole board to every client?**

> **Model Answer:** Maintain a spatial index (a grid or quadtree) over the board's objects keyed by position, and have clients request only the objects intersecting their current viewport bounds, plus a small surrounding margin so minor pans don't trigger a visible load. As a client pans or zooms into a new region, it incrementally requests the newly exposed area rather than reloading anything already held. Real-time broadcast of a mutation also only needs to reach clients whose current viewport includes that object, letting the server filter broadcast per-client viewport rather than blasting every update to everyone regardless of what they can currently see.

**Q: Why should cursor position updates not go through the same path as object edits?**

> **Model Answer:** Cursor updates happen roughly an order of magnitude more often than actual object edits and have no lasting value: a cursor position from half a second ago is simply replaced by the next one, with zero consequence if it's dropped. Object edits are the opposite: infrequent by comparison, but every single one must be delivered and durably recorded, since losing one means losing a real change to the board. Running both through one durable, ordered, retried delivery path means the high-volume disposable stream consumes capacity and can create backpressure that risks delaying or degrading the low-volume stream that actually needs strong guarantees. Separating them lets each be engineered for what it actually needs, best-effort and cheap for cursors, durable and reliable for object mutations.

In a text document, content is one linear sequence, so even a small edit potentially shifts every character after it, which is why text collaborative editing needs OT or CRDT machinery to resolve position conflicts. A whiteboard object's position, size, and style are independent properties on an independent entity with a stable id; moving object A never changes object B's coordinates. This means two users editing two different objects at the same time aren't in conflict at all, they're just two independent deltas that can both apply directly with no merge logic needed. Conflict only exists when two users mutate the exact same object's same property concurrently, a narrower and easier problem.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Per-object independent deltas: the common case (different users editing different objects) needs zero conflict resolution, which is a materially simpler baseline than a shared linear document's merge problem
- Same-object concurrent edits still need a resolution rule (e.g. last-write-wins per property, using a server-assigned or logical timestamp), which is simple to implement but can silently drop one user's concurrent edit to the very same property of the very same object, an accepted, narrow trade-off given how rare that specific collision is in practice
- A CRDT-based approach per-object (each property change tagged with a version vector, merged rather than overwritten) removes even that narrow last-write-wins loss, at the cost of extra metadata per object and more complex client logic, generally justified only if offline editing with later merge is a hard requirement

### Viewport-based partial sync for a large canvas
Sending an entire board's objects to every client on load doesn't scale once boards have thousands of objects, most of which aren't currently visible to any given viewer. Instead, the server maintains a spatial index (e.g. a grid or quadtree keyed by object position) over the board's objects, and a client requests only the objects intersecting its current viewport bounds. As a user pans or zooms, the client requests the newly-exposed region incrementally rather than reloading the board. Real-time updates for objects outside a client's current viewport can be safely skipped or queued at lower priority, since the client can't see them anyway.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Full board load on open: simplest to implement and means a client always has every object in memory ready for any pan/zoom with no extra round trip, but doesn't scale past a moderate object count, and wastes bandwidth loading objects a user may never scroll to
- Viewport-scoped spatial queries with incremental loading on pan/zoom: scales to very large boards and keeps initial load fast, at the cost of a brief loading flicker when panning into a previously-unloaded region, and real-time updates now need to be filtered per-client by what's in their current viewport rather than blindly broadcast to everyone
- A hybrid used in practice: eagerly load a margin beyond the current viewport (so small pans don't trigger a visible load), and fall back to full-board load transparently for boards under some object-count threshold where the added complexity isn't worth it

### Separating cursor/presence broadcast from object-mutation broadcast
Cursor position updates happen far more frequently than actual object edits (per the capacity math, roughly 10x the event rate) and carry no lasting value, a stale cursor position from half a second ago is simply irrelevant once a newer one arrives, unlike an object mutation which must never be lost. Routing both through the same durable, ordered, at-least-once delivery path would mean the high-frequency, disposable cursor stream competes for the same infrastructure guarantees (durability, ordering, retry) that the low-frequency, correctness-critical object stream actually needs, and under load, that competition risks degrading the path that matters.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- One unified event stream for both cursor and object updates: simpler to build (one channel, one delivery guarantee), but forces the correctness-critical object-mutation path to share capacity and backpressure behavior with 10x the volume of throwaway cursor events
- Two separate paths, ephemeral best-effort for cursor/presence (fine to drop or coalesce under load, often UDP-like or a lightweight non-durable pub/sub) and durable at-least-once for object mutations (persisted, retried, ordered): correctly isolates the two very different reliability needs, at the cost of more moving infrastructure pieces to build and operate
- Coalescing cursor updates (only sending the latest position within a throttle window, e.g. 20 times/sec instead of raw mousemove rate) further cuts the 6 million events/sec figure without any loss of perceived smoothness, since human perception can't distinguish a coalesced 20Hz cursor update from a raw one

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Cursor/presence broadcast volume (roughly 10x object-mutation volume in the estimation above) is the single highest-frequency traffic in the system and must be architecturally isolated (separate ephemeral path, client-side throttling/coalescing) so it can never degrade the durable object-mutation path under load.
- A very large board (tens of thousands of objects) stresses the spatial index and the viewport-query path; the index needs to support efficient range queries as objects move (a moved object's index entry must update), not just efficient lookup of static positions.
- A board with unusually high concurrent editor counts (a large live workshop) multiplies both mutation and cursor broadcast fan-out on that one board; this resembles a hotspot problem and may need that specific board's traffic isolated onto dedicated capacity rather than sharing a general pool sized for the 3-editor average case.
- The object_mutations durable log grows without bound for a long-lived, heavily-edited board; like other append-only history logs, it benefits from time-based partitioning and, for undo/redo (which typically only needs recent history), a bounded recent-window cache separate from full historical storage.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Treating every concurrent edit as a conflict== requiring merge logic, when most concurrent edits are on different objects and need no resolution at all.
- ⚠️ ==Loading and syncing an entire board's objects== on every client, which doesn't scale once boards grow past a modest object count.
- ⚠️ Routing cursor/presence updates through the same durable, ordered delivery path as object mutations, letting a 10x-higher-frequency disposable stream compete with correctness-critical traffic.
- ⚠️ Persisting every cursor position update to a database, which is unnecessary write load for data that's irrelevant the instant a newer update arrives.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is syncing a whiteboard fundamentally easier than syncing a shared text document, even though both are 'real-time collaborative editing'?**

> **Model Answer:** A text document is one linear sequence, so any insertion or deletion can shift the meaning of every subsequent position, which is why concurrent text edits need OT or CRDT machinery to resolve. A whiteboard's objects each have their own independent position, size, and properties tied to a stable id; moving one object has zero effect on any other object's data. That means the common case, two users editing two different objects at the same time, requires no conflict resolution at all, they're just two independent deltas. The only remaining conflict case is two users editing the exact same property of the exact same object concurrently, a much narrower problem that a simple last-write-wins rule handles adequately.

**Q: How would you design sync for a board with 50,000 objects without sending the whole board to every client?**

> **Model Answer:** Maintain a spatial index (a grid or quadtree) over the board's objects keyed by position, and have clients request only the objects intersecting their current viewport bounds, plus a small surrounding margin so minor pans don't trigger a visible load. As a client pans or zooms into a new region, it incrementally requests the newly exposed area rather than reloading anything already held. Real-time broadcast of a mutation also only needs to reach clients whose current viewport includes that object, letting the server filter broadcast per-client viewport rather than blasting every update to everyone regardless of what they can currently see.

**Q: Why should cursor position updates not go through the same path as object edits?**

> **Model Answer:** Cursor updates happen roughly an order of magnitude more often than actual object edits and have no lasting value: a cursor position from half a second ago is simply replaced by the next one, with zero consequence if it's dropped. Object edits are the opposite: infrequent by comparison, but every single one must be delivered and durably recorded, since losing one means losing a real change to the board. Running both through one durable, ordered, retried delivery path means the high-volume disposable stream consumes capacity and can create backpressure that risks delaying or degrading the low-volume stream that actually needs strong guarantees. Separating them lets each be engineered for what it actually needs, best-effort and cheap for cursors, durable and reliable for object mutations.

# Design a Version Control System's Backend (Git at Scale)

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `GitHub • GitLab` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Every object in the system, a file's contents, a directory tree, a commit, is identified by **the hash of its own bytes**, so the entire history of a repository is really just a graph of ==immutable, deduplicated, content-addressed== blobs, and almost every hard design question here reduces to how you store and traverse that graph efficiently at huge scale.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design the backend that hosts a distributed version control system like
Git at scale: millions of repositories, some with decades of history and
millions of files (a large monorepo), supporting clone, push, pull, commit
history browsing, and diffs, served to millions of developers and CI jobs
a day. Design the storage and serving system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Are we designing the storage engine for a single huge monorepo, or hosting many independent, mostly-small repositories?
*Why it matters:* A single monorepo with millions of files and a long history stresses tree traversal and partial clone/checkout. Hosting millions of small independent repos stresses multi-tenant storage isolation and sheer repository count. The bottleneck, and the design, differs a lot between the two.

#### Q: Do clients need the full history on every clone, or is a shallow/partial clone acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Full clones of a repository with years of history and huge binary assets can be gigabytes. If most developers and CI jobs only need recent history or a subset of the tree, that unlocks **partial clone** and lazy object fetching, which changes what the server needs to serve efficiently.

#### Q: How write-heavy is this? Are pushes mostly small commits from humans, or does it include high-frequency automated commits from CI/bots?
*Why it matters:* Human push volume is modest and bursty. Automated, high-frequency commits (bots, generated code, CI-driven merges) change the profile toward much higher write QPS and much more aggressive packfile/garbage-collection pressure.

#### Q: Do we need to support large binary files (images, models, build artifacts) well, or is this primarily text/code?
*Why it matters:* Git's delta compression works well on text but poorly on large binaries, which don't diff cleanly. This decides whether the design needs a separate large-file storage path (like Git LFS) pointing out of the main object store.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A developer can clone a repository, getting its full (or partial) history and current file tree.
- A developer can push new commits to a repository and pull new commits made by others.
- A developer can browse commit history and view a diff between any two commits.
- The system can compute and serve the file tree at any specific commit efficiently, not just the latest one.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Storage must scale to hundreds of millions of repositories and, for the largest monorepos, tens of millions of objects and files within a single repository.**
- **Cloning and fetching must be bandwidth-efficient: don't retransmit content the client's data already has or that hasn't changed.**
- **High durability: a repository's committed history must never be lost or silently corrupted, since it is often a project's entire source of truth.**
- **The object store must deduplicate identical content across commits, branches, and even across unrelated repositories, since source trees share enormous amounts of near-identical text.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 100 million repositories total; the top 1,000 are large monorepos with 10 million objects and 50 GB of history each
- 50 million pushes per day platform-wide, averaging 5 changed objects (blob + tree + commit) per push
- An average object (blob/tree/commit) is 2 KB after compression
- 10 million clone/fetch operations per day, averaging 20 MB of data transferred per operation after delta compression

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Objects written per day:** 50,000,000 pushes * 5 objects = 250 million new objects/day ≈ 2,900 object writes/sec average
- **Raw new storage per day before compaction:** 250,000,000 objects * 2 KB = ~500 GB/day of loose object writes, before packfile compaction removes redundancy
- **Fetch/clone bandwidth per day:** 10,000,000 fetches * 20 MB = 200,000 GB (200 TB) of egress/day, which is the dominant infrastructure cost, not the writes
- **A single large monorepo's object count:** 10 million objects at 2 KB average = ~20 GB of loose objects, but real-world packed monorepos compress far below this via delta encoding against similar blobs, which is exactly why packfiles exist

*Capacity Takeaway:* The system is **read/bandwidth-dominated**, not write-dominated (200 TB/day served vs 500 GB/day written), so the entire storage design centers on making stored objects small (delta compression into packfiles) and making fetches send only what a client doesn't already have (negotiation over what commits/objects the client already has), rather than on write throughput.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Every write starts from a client-computed set of content-addressed
objects: file contents hashed into blobs, directory listings hashed into
trees, and a commit hashing a tree plus parent commit(s) plus metadata. A
push sends only the objects the server doesn't already have (negotiated by
SHA) packed into one packfile, and finishes with an atomic ref update
(moving a branch pointer from old SHA to new SHA), which is the only
moment concurrent pushes to the same branch can conflict, cheaply detected
as a compare-and-swap failure. A fetch/clone works in reverse: the client
tells the server which commits it already has, the server walks the
object graph to find everything reachable from the requested ref but not
reachable from the client's haves, and streams just that delta as a
packfile. In the background, a repacking/garbage-collection job merges
loose objects into larger delta-compressed packfiles and removes objects
no longer reachable from any ref, keeping storage bounded despite history
never being edited in place.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Push and fetch through content-addressed object storage

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Git Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    gitserver["Git Protocol Servers"]:::server
    refdb[("Refs DB")]:::db
    objindex[("Object Index")]:::db
    objstore["Object / Pack Storage"]:::server
    gcworker["Repack / GC Worker"]:::server
    client --> lb
    lb --> gitserver
    gitserver -->|"read/CAS ref"| refdb
    gitserver -->|"lookup/write SHA"| objindex
    gitserver -->|"read/write objects"| objstore
    gcworker -.->|"compact + collect"| objstore
    gcworker -.->|"update index"| objindex
```

#### Anatomy of a push

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Client computes new objects (hash blobs, trees, commit locally)"]:::step
    step_2["2. Client sends its ref state (what commits does it already share with server)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Server computes missing objects (graph diff between client and server refs)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Client uploads only missing objects (packed into one packfile)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Server validates objects (hash verification, permission check)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. Server atomically updates ref (compare-and-swap old SHA to new SHA)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
```

#### Loose objects vs packed storage over ten days of pushes

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/{repo}/git-upload-pack` | The fetch/clone protocol endpoint. Client advertises which commits it already has (its 'haves'); server computes the minimal set of missing objects and streams them back as a packfile. |
| `POST` | `/{repo}/git-receive-pack` | The push protocol endpoint. Client streams a packfile of new objects plus the ref update (e.g. 'move main from commit A to commit B'); server validates, stores objects, and atomically updates the ref. |
| `GET` | `/api/repos/{repo}/commits/{sha}` | Returns commit metadata (author, message, parent commit(s), tree SHA) for browsing history in a web UI, without requiring a full clone. |
| `GET` | `/api/repos/{repo}/diff` | Params: base_sha, head_sha. Computes and returns a diff between two commits' trees for web-based code review. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `objects`
- `sha (content hash, primary key)`
- `type (blob | tree | commit | tag)`
- `compressed_bytes or packfile_pointer`
- `size_bytes`
*Notes:* The single content-addressed store underlying everything. A blob is file content, a tree is a directory listing (names mapping to blob/tree SHAs), a commit points to one tree and one or more parent commits. Identical content anywhere, any file, any repo, hashes to the same SHA and is stored once.

### Entity: `refs`
- `repo_id (indexed)`
- `ref_name (e.g. refs/heads/main)`
- `target_sha`
- `updated_at`
*Notes:* The only mutable pointers in the whole system; a branch is nothing but a ref name pointing at a commit SHA, and pushing a commit is really just an atomic compare-and-swap on this pointer.

### Entity: `packfiles`
- `pack_id`
- `repo_id (indexed)`
- `object_shas_index (which SHAs live in this pack, and at what offset)`
- `storage_location`
*Notes:* Periodically, many loose objects are compacted into one delta-compressed packfile, since storing a file's history as a chain of small diffs against a similar base object is far smaller than storing each full version.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Content-addressable storage and deduplication: why hash-based object IDs instead of sequential IDs
Every object's ID is the cryptographic hash of its own content. This means two files with identical content, anywhere in a repo's history, across branches, or even in a completely unrelated repository on the same server, hash to the same ID and are stored exactly once. It also makes corruption self-evident: if an object's bytes don't hash to its claimed ID, it's provably corrupt, no separate checksum bookkeeping needed.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Content-addressing: automatic deduplication across the entire object store, and built-in integrity verification, at the cost of needing a global object-lookup index (a large hash table) that must stay fast even at billions of objects
- Sequential auto-increment object IDs: trivially fast to generate and index, but no deduplication at all, an unchanged file copied into ten commits would be stored ten times, and corruption requires a separate checksum layer to detect
- Cross-repository deduplication at platform scale (a common open-source license file, a common dependency lockfile appearing in millions of repos) is enormous in aggregate, which is why hosts like GitHub really do dedupe objects across repos under the hood, not just within one

### Packfiles and garbage collection: bounding storage growth for history that's never edited
Committed history is immutable, nothing is ever deleted from a normal push, so ==storage would grow forever== if every object stayed a separate loose file. **Packfiles** solve the size problem: many objects are grouped together and stored as one base object plus a chain of small binary deltas against similar objects (a new version of a file delta-encoded against its previous version), which for text-heavy repos is dramatically smaller than storing each full version. Garbage collection solves the growth problem: it finds objects unreachable from any ref (e.g. from a deleted branch or an amended, orphaned commit) and removes them, since content-addressing alone doesn't know an object is no longer wanted.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Aggressive periodic repacking: much smaller storage footprint and faster fetches (delta chains are compact), but repacking a huge monorepo's full object graph is CPU and I/O intensive and must run as an offline background job, not inline on every push
- Never repacking, keeping every object loose: writes stay trivially simple, but storage grows close to linearly with raw history size and fetches transfer far more bytes than necessary
- Garbage collection has a real safety trade-off: run it too aggressively and a commit that's momentarily unreachable (e.g. mid-rebase, before a client's local ref catches up) can be deleted before it's needed again, which is why real systems use a grace period (like Git's reflog expiry window) before permanently removing unreachable objects

### Serving a huge monorepo efficiently: partial clone and lazy object fetching
A naive clone walks the entire reachable object graph from history's very first commit, which for a monorepo with millions of files and years of history can mean gigabytes transferred and minutes of server-side graph walking before a developer can even start working. Partial clone changes the contract: the client gets full commit and tree history (small, since trees/commits are lightweight metadata) but blob content is fetched lazily, only when a file is actually checked out or opened, and shallow clone additionally truncates history depth entirely.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Full clone: simplest mental model, works fully offline afterward, but for a large monorepo can mean an unacceptably slow first clone and huge local disk usage most developers never actually need
- Partial clone (blobs on demand): dramatically faster initial clone and less local storage, but requires the client to stay connected to fetch blobs it doesn't have yet, which breaks fully offline workflows for files outside the working set
- Shallow clone (truncated history depth): fastest and smallest of all, ideal for CI jobs that only need the current snapshot to build, but loses the ability to browse or bisect deep history without a separate, explicit unshallow fetch

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The object-lookup index (SHA to storage location) must serve extremely high read QPS with low latency across billions of objects; it typically needs its own distributed, sharded index rather than living as a column in a general-purpose database.
- A single repository's push traffic is bottlenecked by the atomic ref-update step, since concurrent pushes to the same branch must serialize through a compare-and-swap; high-contention branches (a huge team pushing to the same default branch) may need server-side push queuing to avoid client-visible retry storms.
- Background repacking and garbage collection for the very largest monorepos is itself a scaling problem, since walking a graph with tens of millions of objects and reachability-checking every one takes real time and I/O, and must be scheduled to avoid competing with live push/fetch traffic.
- Fetch bandwidth (200 TB/day in this estimate) dominates infrastructure cost, so CDN-style caching of popular packfiles (frequently-fetched branches, tags, and releases) and geographically distributed mirrors matter more here than almost anywhere else in the design.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Treating a commit as a snapshot copy of the whole file tree rather than understanding that trees and blobs are shared and deduplicated across commits, leading to wildly overestimated storage costs.
- ⚠️ Designing garbage collection to run inline on every push instead of as an offline background job, which would make every push latency-sensitive to a full reachability walk of the object graph.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that push conflicts are resolved at the ref level (a compare-and-swap on a branch pointer), and instead designing complicated per-file locking that Git's actual model doesn't need.
- ⚠️ Assuming every clone needs full history and full blob content, missing that partial and shallow clone exist specifically because large monorepos and CI jobs usually don't need either.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does content-addressable storage matter more here than in most other systems?**

> **Model Answer:** Because source code across commits, branches, and even unrelated repositories is enormously repetitive, most of a file's content is unchanged from its previous version, and many files (license text, common config, vendored dependencies) are byte-identical across projects entirely. Hashing objects by content means all of that repetition collapses into single stored copies automatically, with no separate deduplication pass needed, and as a side effect any corrupted object is instantly detectable because its bytes no longer match its claimed hash.

**Q: Why is a push modeled as an atomic ref update rather than a direct file write?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the actual mutable state in the whole system is tiny: a ref is just a pointer (a branch name mapped to a commit SHA). The objects a push adds are immutable and can be written first, at leisure, with no risk of a bad partial state, since nothing else points at them yet. Only the final ref update, moving the branch pointer to the new commit, needs to be atomic and conflict-checked (via compare-and-swap against the ref's expected old value), which is far simpler and cheaper than making the whole object write path transactional.

**Q: Why would you introduce partial clone for a large monorepo instead of just optimizing packfile compression?**

> **Model Answer:** Because compression only reduces the size of what you're sending, it doesn't reduce how much you're sending. A monorepo with millions of files means most developers only ever touch a small working set, so transferring and storing locally every blob for every file that's ever existed in history is wasted bandwidth and disk regardless of how well it compresses. Partial clone changes what's fetched at all, not how efficiently it's packed, which is a fundamentally bigger win for repositories at that scale.

*Capacity Takeaway:* The system is **read/bandwidth-dominated**, not write-dominated (200 TB/day served vs 500 GB/day written), so the entire storage design centers on making stored objects small (delta compression into packfiles) and making fetches send only what a client doesn't already have (negotiation over what commits/objects the client already has), rather than on write throughput.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Every write starts from a client-computed set of content-addressed
objects: file contents hashed into blobs, directory listings hashed into
trees, and a commit hashing a tree plus parent commit(s) plus metadata. A
push sends only the objects the server doesn't already have (negotiated by
SHA) packed into one packfile, and finishes with an atomic ref update
(moving a branch pointer from old SHA to new SHA), which is the only
moment concurrent pushes to the same branch can conflict, cheaply detected
as a compare-and-swap failure. A fetch/clone works in reverse: the client
tells the server which commits it already has, the server walks the
object graph to find everything reachable from the requested ref but not
reachable from the client's haves, and streams just that delta as a
packfile. In the background, a repacking/garbage-collection job merges
loose objects into larger delta-compressed packfiles and removes objects
no longer reachable from any ref, keeping storage bounded despite history
never being edited in place.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Push and fetch through content-addressed object storage

```mermaid

    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/{repo}/git-upload-pack` | The fetch/clone protocol endpoint. Client advertises which commits it already has (its 'haves'); server computes the minimal set of missing objects and streams them back as a packfile. |
| `POST` | `/{repo}/git-receive-pack` | The push protocol endpoint. Client streams a packfile of new objects plus the ref update (e.g. 'move main from commit A to commit B'); server validates, stores objects, and atomically updates the ref. |
| `GET` | `/api/repos/{repo}/commits/{sha}` | Returns commit metadata (author, message, parent commit(s), tree SHA) for browsing history in a web UI, without requiring a full clone. |
| `GET` | `/api/repos/{repo}/diff` | Params: base_sha, head_sha. Computes and returns a diff between two commits' trees for web-based code review. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `objects`
- `sha (content hash, primary key)`
- `type (blob | tree | commit | tag)`
- `compressed_bytes or packfile_pointer`
- `size_bytes`
*Notes:* The single content-addressed store underlying everything. A blob is file content, a tree is a directory listing (names mapping to blob/tree SHAs), a commit points to one tree and one or more parent commits. Identical content anywhere, any file, any repo, hashes to the same SHA and is stored once.

### Entity: `refs`
- `repo_id (indexed)`
- `ref_name (e.g. refs/heads/main)`
- `target_sha`
- `updated_at`
*Notes:* The only mutable pointers in the whole system; a branch is nothing but a ref name pointing at a commit SHA, and pushing a commit is really just an atomic compare-and-swap on this pointer.

### Entity: `packfiles`
- `pack_id`
- `repo_id (indexed)`
- `object_shas_index (which SHAs live in this pack, and at what offset)`
- `storage_location`
*Notes:* Periodically, many loose objects are compacted into one delta-compressed packfile, since storing a file's history as a chain of small diffs against a similar base object is far smaller than storing each full version.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Content-addressable storage and deduplication: why hash-based object IDs instead of sequential IDs
Every object's ID is the cryptographic hash of its own content. This means two files with identical content, anywhere in a repo's history, across branches, or even in a completely unrelated repository on the same server, hash to the same ID and are stored exactly once. It also makes corruption self-evident: if an object's bytes don't hash to its claimed ID, it's provably corrupt, no separate checksum bookkeeping needed.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Content-addressing: automatic deduplication across the entire object store, and built-in integrity verification, at the cost of needing a global object-lookup index (a large hash table) that must stay fast even at billions of objects
- Sequential auto-increment object IDs: trivially fast to generate and index, but no deduplication at all, an unchanged file copied into ten commits would be stored ten times, and corruption requires a separate checksum layer to detect
- Cross-repository deduplication at platform scale (a common open-source license file, a common dependency lockfile appearing in millions of repos) is enormous in aggregate, which is why hosts like GitHub really do dedupe objects across repos under the hood, not just within one

### Packfiles and garbage collection: bounding storage growth for history that's never edited
Committed history is immutable, nothing is ever deleted from a normal push, so ==storage would grow forever== if every object stayed a separate loose file. **Packfiles** solve the size problem: many objects are grouped together and stored as one base object plus a chain of small binary deltas against similar objects (a new version of a file delta-encoded against its previous version), which for text-heavy repos is dramatically smaller than storing each full version. Garbage collection solves the growth problem: it finds objects unreachable from any ref (e.g. from a deleted branch or an amended, orphaned commit) and removes them, since content-addressing alone doesn't know an object is no longer wanted.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Aggressive periodic repacking: much smaller storage footprint and faster fetches (delta chains are compact), but repacking a huge monorepo's full object graph is CPU and I/O intensive and must run as an offline background job, not inline on every push
- Never repacking, keeping every object loose: writes stay trivially simple, but storage grows close to linearly with raw history size and fetches transfer far more bytes than necessary
- Garbage collection has a real safety trade-off: run it too aggressively and a commit that's momentarily unreachable (e.g. mid-rebase, before a client's local ref catches up) can be deleted before it's needed again, which is why real systems use a grace period (like Git's reflog expiry window) before permanently removing unreachable objects

### Serving a huge monorepo efficiently: partial clone and lazy object fetching
A naive clone walks the entire reachable object graph from history's very first commit, which for a monorepo with millions of files and years of history can mean gigabytes transferred and minutes of server-side graph walking before a developer can even start working. Partial clone changes the contract: the client gets full commit and tree history (small, since trees/commits are lightweight metadata) but blob content is fetched lazily, only when a file is actually checked out or opened, and shallow clone additionally truncates history depth entirely.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Full clone: simplest mental model, works fully offline afterward, but for a large monorepo can mean an unacceptably slow first clone and huge local disk usage most developers never actually need
- Partial clone (blobs on demand): dramatically faster initial clone and less local storage, but requires the client to stay connected to fetch blobs it doesn't have yet, which breaks fully offline workflows for files outside the working set
- Shallow clone (truncated history depth): fastest and smallest of all, ideal for CI jobs that only need the current snapshot to build, but loses the ability to browse or bisect deep history without a separate, explicit unshallow fetch

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The object-lookup index (SHA to storage location) must serve extremely high read QPS with low latency across billions of objects; it typically needs its own distributed, sharded index rather than living as a column in a general-purpose database.
- A single repository's push traffic is bottlenecked by the atomic ref-update step, since concurrent pushes to the same branch must serialize through a compare-and-swap; high-contention branches (a huge team pushing to the same default branch) may need server-side push queuing to avoid client-visible retry storms.
- Background repacking and garbage collection for the very largest monorepos is itself a scaling problem, since walking a graph with tens of millions of objects and reachability-checking every one takes real time and I/O, and must be scheduled to avoid competing with live push/fetch traffic.
- Fetch bandwidth (200 TB/day in this estimate) dominates infrastructure cost, so CDN-style caching of popular packfiles (frequently-fetched branches, tags, and releases) and geographically distributed mirrors matter more here than almost anywhere else in the design.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Treating a commit as a snapshot copy of the whole file tree rather than understanding that trees and blobs are shared and deduplicated across commits, leading to wildly overestimated storage costs.
- ⚠️ Designing garbage collection to run inline on every push instead of as an offline background job, which would make every push latency-sensitive to a full reachability walk of the object graph.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that push conflicts are resolved at the ref level (a compare-and-swap on a branch pointer), and instead designing complicated per-file locking that Git's actual model doesn't need.
- ⚠️ Assuming every clone needs full history and full blob content, missing that partial and shallow clone exist specifically because large monorepos and CI jobs usually don't need either.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does content-addressable storage matter more here than in most other systems?**

> **Model Answer:** Because source code across commits, branches, and even unrelated repositories is enormously repetitive, most of a file's content is unchanged from its previous version, and many files (license text, common config, vendored dependencies) are byte-identical across projects entirely. Hashing objects by content means all of that repetition collapses into single stored copies automatically, with no separate deduplication pass needed, and as a side effect any corrupted object is instantly detectable because its bytes no longer match its claimed hash.

**Q: Why is a push modeled as an atomic ref update rather than a direct file write?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the actual mutable state in the whole system is tiny: a ref is just a pointer (a branch name mapped to a commit SHA). The objects a push adds are immutable and can be written first, at leisure, with no risk of a bad partial state, since nothing else points at them yet. Only the final ref update, moving the branch pointer to the new commit, needs to be atomic and conflict-checked (via compare-and-swap against the ref's expected old value), which is far simpler and cheaper than making the whole object write path transactional.

**Q: Why would you introduce partial clone for a large monorepo instead of just optimizing packfile compression?**

> **Model Answer:** Because compression only reduces the size of what you're sending, it doesn't reduce how much you're sending. A monorepo with millions of files means most developers only ever touch a small working set, so transferring and storing locally every blob for every file that's ever existed in history is wasted bandwidth and disk regardless of how well it compresses. Partial clone changes what's fetched at all, not how efficiently it's packed, which is a fundamentally bigger win for repositories at that scale.

lesson.content:
# Design a Distributed Database (from Scratch, General)

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `CockroachDB • Google Spanner` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A single machine gives you consistency, availability, and simplicity for free; the moment you spread data across a network, **CAP theorem** forces you to give up availability or consistency during a partition, and every other decision in this design, how you shard, how you replicate, how you commit a transaction, is really just a consequence of which side of that trade-off you deliberately chose.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a distributed database from scratch: a system that stores data
across many machines, supports reads and writes with a chosen consistency
guarantee, survives individual node failures without losing committed
data, and can execute transactions that span multiple partitions of data.
Design the storage and coordination layers end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Do we need strong (linearizable) consistency, or is eventual/causal consistency acceptable for this workload?
*Why it matters:* This is the single decision CAP theorem forces explicitly: under a network partition, a strongly consistent system must ==refuse some requests== to avoid returning stale or conflicting data, while an eventually consistent one stays available and reconciles later. It determines the replication protocol, the read path, and the failure behavior for the entire system.

#### Q: Do transactions need to span multiple shards/partitions, or is single-shard (single-key or single-partition) atomicity enough?
*Why it matters:* Single-shard transactions are cheap, a partition can just use a local lock and a write-ahead log. Cross-shard transactions require **distributed coordination** (two-phase commit or a similar protocol), which adds real latency and a whole new failure mode: a coordinator crashing mid-commit.

#### Q: What's the read/write ratio, and how large is the dataset relative to what a single node could hold?
*Why it matters:* If the data fits on one beefy machine, partitioning is unnecessary complexity. Partitioning only earns its cost once the dataset or the write throughput genuinely exceeds one machine's capacity, which is the actual justification for sharding at all.

#### Q: What failure modes must we tolerate: single node crashes, whole rack/datacenter loss, or network partitions between regions?
*Why it matters:* Tolerating a single node crash needs only local replication (a handful of replicas in one datacenter). Tolerating a full datacenter loss needs geo-replication across regions, which multiplies write latency because a majority of geographically distant replicas must acknowledge every write.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Clients can read and write individual keys/rows, with data distributed (sharded) across many nodes.
- The system replicates every piece of data onto multiple nodes so a single node failure doesn't lose or block access to data.
- The system supports transactions that atomically read and write multiple keys, including keys on different shards.
- The system detects and recovers from node failure automatically, promoting a replica to take over without operator intervention.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **The system must survive the loss of any single node (and ideally a whole availability zone) without ==losing any committed write==.**
- **The system must state and hold to an explicit **consistency model** (e.g. linearizable, or bounded-staleness) rather than leaving it ambiguous, since every client-facing guarantee depends on it.**
- **Write latency for a cross-shard transaction must stay bounded (low tens of milliseconds within one region) even though it requires coordination across multiple nodes.**
- **The system must scale horizontally: adding nodes should increase both storage capacity and write throughput roughly linearly, not require a full re-architecture.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 10 TB of active data, growing to 100 TB within two years
- 50,000 writes/sec and 200,000 reads/sec sustained, at peak roughly 3x that
- Each row/record averages 1 KB; data is replicated 3x for durability
- 10% of writes are cross-shard transactions touching an average of 3 shards

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Total data with replication:** 100 TB * 3 replicas = 300 TB of total stored bytes at the two-year mark
- **Shard count and size:** Target ~50 GB per shard for manageable rebalancing and recovery time: 100 TB / 50 GB = 2,000 shards, each replicated 3x = 6,000 shard-replicas to place across the cluster
- **Write throughput per shard:** 50,000 writes/sec / 2,000 shards = 25 writes/sec/shard average, comfortably low per shard even though the aggregate is high, confirming sharding by key range/hash successfully spreads load
- **Cross-shard transaction volume:** 50,000 writes/sec * 10% = **5,000 cross-shard transactions/sec**, each needing coordination across ~3 shards, meaning ~15,000 extra inter-node coordination messages/sec just for distributed commit

*Capacity Takeaway:* The dominant scaling driver isn't raw data volume, 300 TB spread over 2,000 shards is unremarkable, it's the 5,000/sec cross-shard transactions, since each one requires multi-node coordination (not just a local write), and that ==coordination cost==, not storage or single-shard throughput, is what determines the system's actual write latency and ceiling.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Data is partitioned into shards by key range or consistent hash, and each
shard is independently replicated (typically 3 or 5 replicas) via a
consensus protocol like Raft, giving each shard its own leader that
serializes writes and a log that followers replay to stay in sync; a
single-shard write only needs that shard's own replica group to agree,
which keeps most writes cheap. A cross-shard transaction adds a
coordination layer on top: a coordinator (often just the client, or a
dedicated transaction manager) runs **two-phase commit** across every shard
the transaction touches, first asking each shard's leader to durably
prepare its part of the write (locking the affected keys and persisting
an intent), then, only once every participant has confirmed prepare,
telling all of them to commit. Node failure is handled at the consensus
layer: if a shard's leader dies, its replica group elects a new leader
from the surviving replicas using the same consensus protocol, and no
committed write is lost because it was already durably replicated to a
majority before being acknowledged.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Sharded, replicated storage with a two-phase commit coordinator

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client / App"]:::client
    router["Routing Layer"]:::server
    shardmap[("Shard Map")]:::db
    shardA[("Shard A (leader+replicas)")]:::db
    shardB[("Shard B (leader+replicas)")]:::db
    shardC[("Shard C (leader+replicas)")]:::db
    coordinator["Txn Coordinator"]:::server
    client --> router
    router -->|"lookup shard"| shardmap
    router -->|"single-shard read/write"| shardA
    router -->|"cross-shard txn"| coordinator
    coordinator -->|"prepare/commit"| shardA
    coordinator -->|"prepare/commit"| shardB
    coordinator -->|"prepare/commit"| shardC
```

#### Two-phase commit across three shards

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/kv/{key}` | Reads the current value for a key; routed by the client (or a routing layer) to the shard owning that key's range/hash, served by that shard's current leader or a bounded-staleness-tolerant replica. |
| `PUT` | `/kv/{key}` | Body: { value }. Writes a key, routed to and committed through the owning shard's replication protocol before acknowledging success. |
| `POST` | `/txn/begin` | Starts a distributed transaction, returning a transaction_id used to scope subsequent reads/writes across one or more shards before commit. |
| `POST` | `/txn/{transaction_id}/commit` | Commits all reads/writes performed under this transaction atomically across every shard touched, using two-phase commit; returns success only once every participating shard has durably prepared and committed. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `shard_map`
- `shard_id`
- `key_range or hash_range (start, end)`
- `replica_node_ids (ordered, leader first)`
- `version (incremented on any rebalance)`
*Notes:* The routing table every client/gateway consults to find which shard, and which node within that shard's replica group, owns a given key. Cached aggressively by clients, but must be strongly consistent itself or ==routing goes stale== during a rebalance.

### Entity: `shard_log (per shard)`
- `log_index (monotonic, per shard)`
- `operation (key, value, op type)`
- `term_or_epoch`
*Notes:* Each shard is really a small **replicated state machine**: a write-ahead log replicated via a consensus protocol (Raft or Paxos) to that shard's replica set, applied in log order to the actual key-value store.

### Entity: `transaction_intents`
- `transaction_id`
- `key, shard_id`
- `proposed_value`
- `status (prepared | committed | aborted)`
*Notes:* Tracks the in-flight, not-yet-finalized writes of a cross-shard transaction during two-phase commit, so a crashed coordinator can be recovered from by inspecting what every participant already prepared.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Partitioning strategy: range-based vs hash-based sharding
**Range-based sharding** assigns contiguous key ranges to shards (e.g. keys 'a' through 'm' on shard 1), which keeps related, sequentially-accessed keys together and makes range scans (e.g. 'all orders from this week') cheap, hitting few shards. **Hash-based sharding** assigns a shard by hashing the key, spreading logically related keys uniformly at random across shards, which avoids hot shards from sequential access patterns (like monotonically increasing IDs all landing on the newest range) but makes range scans expensive, since a scan now has to fan out to nearly every shard.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Range-based: efficient range scans and easy to reason about locality, but vulnerable to hotspotting when access is skewed toward one range (e.g. all writes going to the newest, still-small time-ordered shard)
- Hash-based: naturally load-balances writes across all shards regardless of access pattern, but range queries lose locality entirely and must scatter-gather across many shards
- Production systems often use range-based sharding with automatic, dynamic re-splitting of hot ranges (e.g. CockroachDB's range splitting), getting range-scan locality most of the time while still breaking up emergent hotspots as they appear

### Consistency model: linearizability vs eventual consistency, and living with what CAP actually says
CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between **Consistency** (every read sees the latest committed write, but some requests may be refused/blocked) and **Availability** (every request gets a response, but it might be stale). A linearizable system (like this design's default, using consensus per shard) picks consistency: if a shard's replica group can't reach a majority (a partition isolates the minority), the minority side ==stops serving writes, and even reads==, rather than risk returning stale data. An eventually consistent system picks availability: every replica keeps serving reads and writes even when partitioned, and conflicting writes are reconciled later (last-write-wins, vector clocks, or CRDTs).

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Linearizable (CP): every client sees a single, agreed-upon order of operations, which is what most application developers actually want (no surprising conflicts to resolve), at the cost of unavailability for the minority side of a partition
- Eventually consistent (AP): the system never refuses a request, even mid-partition, which matters for use cases where availability trumps correctness (a shopping cart shouldn't refuse an add-to-cart because of a network blip), at the cost of applications needing to handle conflicting concurrent writes themselves
- This design deliberately chooses CP by using majority-based consensus per shard, which is the right default for a general-purpose database where silent data divergence would be a correctness bug most application teams aren't equipped to reconcile themselves

### Cross-shard transactions: two-phase commit and its actual failure mode
Two-phase commit has a **prepare phase** (the coordinator asks every participating shard to lock the relevant keys, persist an intent, and vote yes/no) and a **commit phase** (once every participant votes yes, the coordinator tells all of them to commit; if any votes no, it tells all of them to abort). The mechanism is straightforward; the actual hard problem is ==coordinator failure==: if the coordinator crashes after some shards have prepared (locked and voted yes) but before it sends the final commit/abort decision, those shards are stuck holding locks indefinitely, unable to unilaterally decide whether to commit or abort, since only the coordinator knew the collective outcome.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Classic two-phase commit: conceptually simple and widely implemented, but a crashed coordinator can leave participants blocked holding locks until it (or a replacement) recovers and reads its own durably-logged decision, which is a real availability cost during coordinator failure
- Making the coordinator itself replicated/durable (its own decision log survives its crash, and a standby can resume from it) removes the indefinite-block risk, at the cost of extra infrastructure and latency for the coordinator's own writes
- Some systems (like Spanner) instead assign one of the participating shards to also act as coordinator rather than a separate service, reducing moving parts, but still need the same durable decision log to recover from a crash mid-commit

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single shard's write throughput is capped by its leader (only the leader accepts writes in most consensus protocols), so a hot key range that can't be split further becomes a ==hard ceiling==; automatic range-splitting on load, not just size, is needed to keep any one shard from becoming a bottleneck.
- Cross-shard transactions scale worse than single-shard writes because **coordination latency** grows with the number of participating shards and the network distance between them; keeping frequently-co-transacted data on the same shard (deliberate co-location) reduces how often cross-shard coordination is even needed.
- The shard map (routing table) itself must stay available and consistent even during rebalancing; a stale shard map served to a client causes requests to hit the wrong node, so rebalancing operations need to update the map atomically and clients need a cheap way to detect and refresh a stale mapping.
- Geo-replication across regions for disaster tolerance multiplies write latency (majority consensus now needs acknowledgment from geographically distant replicas), which is why some systems offer per-table or per-row control over replication placement, so latency-sensitive data isn't forced to pay for global durability it doesn't need.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing the system without ever ==explicitly stating its consistency model==, then being unable to answer what happens to a read during a network partition.
- ⚠️ Assuming sharding alone solves cross-shard transactions, when in fact partitioning data is what creates the cross-shard transaction problem in the first place.
- ⚠️ Forgetting that a two-phase commit coordinator can itself crash mid-protocol, and not designing a durable decision log to recover participants stuck holding locks.
- ⚠️ Choosing hash-based sharding without noting that it sacrifices efficient range scans, or choosing range-based sharding without a plan for splitting hot ranges.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Concretely, what does a network partition force this system to choose, and what did you choose?**

> **Model Answer:** When a partition splits a shard's replica group so no side has a majority, or splits a minority off from the majority, the minority side has to choose: keep serving reads/writes with possibly-stale or conflicting data (availability), or refuse to serve until it can confirm it's talking to a majority (consistency). This design chooses **consistency** by using majority-based consensus per shard: a replica that can't reach a majority stops accepting writes, and typically stops serving linearizable reads too, rather than risk an incorrect answer.

**Q: Why does a cross-shard transaction cost more than the sum of the single-shard writes it contains?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a single-shard write only needs that shard's own replica group to reach consensus, one round of coordination. A cross-shard transaction needs every participating shard to agree on the same outcome (commit or abort) atomically, which requires an additional coordination layer, two-phase commit, on top of each shard's own consensus round. That's an extra round trip (prepare, then commit) across every participant, plus the requirement that a lock be held on every participant's keys for the duration, which single-shard writes never need.

**Q: How would you recover a transaction if the coordinator crashes right after some shards prepared but before any received a commit decision?**

> **Model Answer:** The coordinator must durably log its final decision (commit or abort) before telling any participant, specifically so that after a crash and restart (or takeover by a replacement coordinator), it can read that log and resume by re-sending the same decision to every participant. A participant holding a prepared-but-undecided lock periodically checks back with the coordinator (or a shared decision log) rather than unilaterally deciding, since only the coordinator's durable log knows the actual collective outcome.
